quiz.prompt: What is the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation, and why is it used to report cryo-EM resolution?
quiz.answer: It is the correlation between two independently refined half-maps as a function of spatial frequency, with resolution quoted where it falls to 0.143. Keeping the two half-sets independent prevents overfitting noise from inflating the apparent resolution, giving an honest, reproducible measure.

quiz.prompt: What two technical advances drove the cryo-EM 'resolution revolution,' and what new capability do continuous-heterogeneity methods add?
quiz.answer: Direct-electron detectors (fast frame capture enabling beam-induced-motion correction) and maximum-likelihood/Bayesian refinement (probabilistic weighting of noisy particles, e.g. RELION). Continuous-heterogeneity methods (3D variability, cryoDRGN) go beyond discrete classes to reconstruct continuous conformational landscapes, making cryo-EM a dynamics tool.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Turning a drop of purified protein into an atomic 3D model by cryo-EM is a pipeline, not a single measurement. You flash-freeze the sample into glassy ice, film thousands of noisy movies of individual molecules frozen in random poses, then computationally sort, align, and average them into a sharpening 3D map, and finally build and check an atomic model. Each stage cleans up noise and adds information until atoms emerge from blur.

### Precisely

The **single-particle cryo-EM workflow**:
1. **Vitrification** — plunge-freeze a thin sample film so water becomes glassy (vitreous) ice, preserving native structure.
2. **Movie acquisition & motion correction** — record dose-fractionated movies on a direct electron detector; align frames to undo beam-induced **motion** and apply **CTF** correction.
3. **Particle picking** — extract individual particle images from micrographs.
4. **2D classification** — group similar views, discarding junk.
5. **3D classification & refinement** — sort conformations/orientations and iteratively refine a 3D **map**, assigning each particle's pose.
6. **Validation** — assess resolution by **Fourier shell correlation (FSC)** and build/refine an atomic model.

### Worked example

From, say, a million picked particles, 2D classification weeds out ice contamination and broken particles, leaving clean class averages showing distinct views. 3D classification may reveal *multiple conformations* (a strength of cryo-EM — it captures heterogeneity), each refined separately. Averaging tens of thousands of good particles beats noise down as $\sim1/\sqrt{N}$, pushing the map to ~2–4 Å, where side chains appear and an atomic model can be built and checked against the **Ramachandran** plot.

### Why it's true / how it works

Each particle image is an extremely low-dose (to avoid radiation damage), noisy 2D projection of the 3D object from a random angle. Because projections from all angles are present, assigning each its orientation and back-projecting reconstructs the 3D density; averaging many copies of each view recovers signal buried far below the per-image noise.

### Where it connects

It is the practical realization of the **CTF** correction concept, judged by **FSC** (the **resolution revolution** atom), and complements crystallography (**Bragg**) and **NMR**; resulting maps are interpreted with **Ramachandran** geometry and often flexibly fit with **ENM**/MD.

### Watch out

**Resolution is non-uniform** across a map (flexible regions stay blurry) and **preferred orientation** (particles favouring certain poses) leaves angular gaps that distort reconstructions. The map is a *time- and conformation-average*; over-interpreting a single map ignores the very heterogeneity cryo-EM is best at revealing — which is why 3D classification matters.

### Numbers & nuance

Signal builds statistically: averaging $N$ aligned particles beats noise down as $\sim1/\sqrt{N}$, so reaching atomic resolution typically needs $10^4$–$10^6$ good particles culled from far more picked candidates. **2D classification** discards ice, aggregates, and broken particles; **3D classification** is where cryo-EM shines — it sorts coexisting *conformations* from one dataset, turning sample heterogeneity from a liability into multiple structures. Map quality is reported by **Fourier shell correlation (FSC)**, with the resolution conventionally quoted at FSC = 0.143 between two independently-refined half-maps (the "gold-standard" guard against over-fitting noise). Two practical hazards: **preferred orientation** (particles favouring certain poses) leaves angular gaps that distort the map, and resolution is **non-uniform** — flexible regions stay blurry even when the core is atomic.

atoms.title: The cryo-EM resolution revolution
atoms.summary: Within a few years, single-particle cryo-EM went from a low-resolution 'blobology' to routinely atomic resolution, displacing crystallography for many large and dynamic complexes.

depths.eli5: For decades cryo-EM gave only fuzzy outlines. Then new cameras and smarter software suddenly made it sharp enough to see individual atoms — so scientists could finally solve giant molecular machines that never formed crystals.
depths.core: Around 2013 the convergence of direct-electron detectors and improved image-processing algorithms raised single-particle cryo-EM resolution from ~1 nm to better than 3–4 Å, and by ~2020 to true atomic resolution (~1.2 Å) on favorable samples. Because it needs no crystal and tolerates heterogeneity, cryo-EM unlocked structures of membrane proteins, ribosomes, spliceosomes, viral machines, and large dynamic assemblies that had resisted crystallography for decades — reshaping structural biology and earning the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
depths.deep: The deeper significance is methodological pluralism: cryo-EM, crystallography, NMR, SAXS, and mass spectrometry are now integrated (integrative/hybrid modeling) because each constrains different aspects — high-resolution local geometry, solution flexibility, dynamics, stoichiometry. Cryo-EM's natural access to multiple conformational states (via 3D classification and continuous-heterogeneity methods) makes it the bridge from static structure to functional dynamics, and it feeds the data that train and validate deep-learning structure and dynamics models. The lesson echoes a theme across biophysics: match the method to the observable — and for big, flexible, crystallization-resistant machines, that method became cryo-EM.

atoms.note: Around 2013, new detectors + algorithms brought atomic resolution without crystals; the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry followed. The frontier point: cryo-EM made dynamics and shape-variety ('heterogeneity') first-class, feeding the integrative-modeling and deep-learning era. ('Resolution' = the finest detail you can resolve, in ångströms; 'integrative modeling' = combining several methods' partial data into one model.)

quiz.prompt: What changed around 2013 to trigger the cryo-EM resolution revolution, and why did it matter for structural biology?
quiz.answer: Direct-electron detectors plus improved (Bayesian/maximum-likelihood) image processing raised resolution to near-atomic without needing crystals. This unlocked large, dynamic, membrane, and crystallization-resistant complexes (ribosomes, spliceosomes, viral and membrane machines), reshaping the field.

quiz.prompt: Why is cryo-EM often described as a bridge from static structure to dynamics?
quiz.answer: Because it images many individual particles, 3D and continuous-heterogeneity classification can separate distinct conformational and compositional states from a single dataset — directly revealing the ensemble of functional states rather than one averaged structure, and feeding data to dynamics-aware models.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

For decades, single-particle cryo-EM produced only fuzzy blobs — affectionately mocked as "blobology" — good for overall shape but never atoms. Then, in just a few years around 2013, it leapt to *atomic* resolution and began routinely solving structures that crystallography could never touch: huge, flexible, membrane-embedded machines that won't crystallize. This sudden jump is the **resolution revolution**, and it reshaped structural biology.

### Precisely

The **cryo-EM resolution revolution** denotes the rapid improvement — within a few years — from low-resolution density maps to **near-atomic and atomic** resolution single-particle reconstructions. Two technical advances drove it: **direct electron detectors** (which record fast movies, dramatically improving the signal-to-noise per electron and enabling **motion correction**) and better **image-processing algorithms** (maximum-likelihood classification and refinement that sort heterogeneity and align noisy particles). It earned the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

### Worked example

Before ~2013, a typical single-particle map might reach 10–20 Å — enough to see a complex's outline but no side chains. After direct detectors and new software, the same kind of sample routinely reached 3–4 Å (side chains visible) and, by the 2020s, even sub-2 Å (resolving individual atoms and waters). Membrane proteins, ribosomes, spliceosomes, and viral machines — many *never* crystallized — became solvable, often in *multiple conformations* from one dataset.

### Why it's true / how it works

Direct detectors capture **dose-fractionated movies**, so beam-induced specimen **motion** (which previously smeared images) can be corrected frame-by-frame, and the detector's higher efficiency means more usable signal per fragile, radiation-limited electron. Smarter algorithms then extract structure from images far noisier than crystallography's, and *separate* coexisting conformations rather than requiring a single rigid crystal — turning heterogeneity from a curse into information.

### Where it connects

It is the payoff of the **cryo-EM workflow** and **CTF** correction, validated by **Fourier shell correlation**, and it displaced or complemented **Bragg** crystallography for large, dynamic, and membrane complexes — feeding structures into **MD**, **ENM**, and drug design.

### Watch out

"Atomic resolution" is now *achievable* but not *guaranteed* — resolution still depends on sample quality, size, and rigidity; small or highly flexible proteins remain hard. And published global resolution numbers hide **local** variation: parts of a map may be atomic while flexible regions are far worse.

### Numbers & nuance

The leap was concrete: typical single-particle maps went from ~10–20 Å (shape only, "blobology") around 2012 to ~3–4 Å (side chains visible) within a few years, and to sub-2 Å (individual atoms, ordered waters) by the early 2020s. Two enablers: **direct electron detectors** that record dose-fractionated movies (allowing per-frame motion correction and far better detective quantum efficiency) and **maximum-likelihood** classification/refinement software (RELION, cryoSPARC) that extracts structure from extremely noisy images and separates conformations. Recognized by the 2017 Nobel Prize. The honest caveats: atomic resolution is *achievable*, not guaranteed — it depends on particle size, rigidity, and ice quality — and a single quoted "global resolution" hides large **local** variation across a map.

atoms.title: Machine-learning force fields
atoms.summary: Neural-network potentials trained on quantum-mechanical data promise near-quantum accuracy at near-classical cost — closing the accuracy/speed gap that has long limited molecular simulation.

depths.eli5: Classical simulations use simple spring-and-charge rules that are fast but approximate; quantum calculations are accurate but far too slow for big molecules. A trained neural network learns to mimic the quantum answer, giving you accuracy and speed at once.
depths.core: Empirical force fields use fixed functional forms (bonds, angles, fixed charges, Lennard-Jones) that are cheap but miss polarization, bond breaking, and subtle electronic effects. Machine-learning potentials instead fit a flexible neural network to a database of quantum-mechanical energies and forces, with architectures that build in physical symmetries (translation, rotation, permutation invariance) — e.g. message-passing graph networks on atomic environments. The result approaches quantum accuracy at a tiny fraction of the cost, enabling reactive and polarizable molecular dynamics at scales QM cannot reach.
depths.deep: The central challenge is transferability and the honest-evaluation theme that runs through modern biophysics ML: a potential is only as good as its training distribution, so extrapolation to unsampled chemistries or conformations can fail silently. Benchmarks must use chemically/conformationally disjoint test sets (the same anti-leakage discipline as protein-flexibility and structure benchmarks) and check energy conservation and stability over long trajectories, not just single-point errors. Foundation-model potentials trained across broad chemical space, active learning to target high-uncertainty regions, and Δ-learning (correcting a cheap baseline) are the current frontiers — and physics baselines (classical force fields, simple models) remain the fair yardstick they must beat.

atoms.note: Same discipline as the rest of biophysics ML: control the train/test split (use chemistry and shapes not seen in training) or the benchmark flatters and lies. Per-frame accuracy means little without long simulations that stay stable and conserve energy. ('Force field' = the rulebook for the forces between atoms; 'quantum-mechanical' = computed from first-principles electron physics, accurate but slow.)

quiz.prompt: What gap do machine-learning force fields aim to close, and how do they differ from classical force fields?
quiz.answer: They aim to close the accuracy/cost gap between cheap-but-approximate classical force fields and accurate-but-expensive quantum mechanics. Rather than fixed functional forms, they fit flexible (symmetry-respecting) neural networks to quantum energies and forces, achieving near-quantum accuracy at near-classical cost.

quiz.prompt: Why must ML force fields be benchmarked on chemically and conformationally disjoint test sets, and what beyond single-point error matters?
quiz.answer: Because their accuracy is bounded by the training distribution; testing on data too similar to training (leakage) overstates transferability and hides silent extrapolation failures. Beyond point-wise energy/force error, you must verify long-trajectory stability and energy conservation, since a model can be accurate per-frame yet produce unstable dynamics.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Molecular simulation has long faced a painful trade-off. Quantum mechanics is accurate but so slow it can only handle a few hundred atoms for a few picoseconds. Classical force fields are fast enough for big biomolecules and long times but are crude approximations that can't break bonds or capture subtle electronics. **Machine-learning force fields** aim to get the best of both: learn the quantum-accurate energy surface from data, then evaluate it at nearly classical speed.

### Precisely

A **machine-learning force field (MLFF)** is a neural network (often a **graph/equivariant** model that respects physical symmetries) trained on **quantum-mechanical** (e.g. DFT) reference energies and forces for many atomic configurations. Once trained, it predicts the potential energy $U(\mathbf{r})$ and atomic forces for new configurations far faster than solving the quantum problem, while approaching quantum **accuracy**. It then drops into **molecular dynamics** in place of a hand-tuned classical force field.

### Worked example

To study a reaction that classical force fields *cannot* describe (because it makes and breaks covalent bonds), train an MLFF on thousands of DFT calculations spanning the reactant, transition state, and product geometries. The trained model then runs nanosecond MD that correctly forms and breaks bonds — capturing chemistry a fixed-bond classical force field is blind to — at a tiny fraction of the cost of running DFT on the fly (ab-initio MD).

### Why it's true / how it works

The potential energy is, in principle, a smooth function of atomic positions; a sufficiently expressive network trained on enough quantum data can *interpolate* that function. Building in physical symmetries (translation, rotation, permutation **equivariance**) and locality lets the model **generalize** and **transfer** to system sizes and configurations beyond the training set, which is the key to usefulness.

### Where it connects

MLFFs upgrade the accuracy of **molecular dynamics** and the **free-energy methods** (FEP, umbrella sampling) built on it, are trained and benchmarked on large datasets (like **mdCATH** in spirit, plus quantum-chemistry datasets), and complement **ENM** (cheap, coarse) at the opposite, high-accuracy end.

### Watch out

MLFFs are only reliable **within their training distribution** — encounter a geometry unlike anything in the training set (a rare transition state, an unusual environment) and predictions can fail silently or unphysically. Generating sufficient, well-sampled quantum reference data is the real bottleneck, and **extrapolation** beyond that data is where these models are most dangerous.

### Numbers & nuance

MLFFs aim to collapse the long-standing accuracy/speed trade-off: quantum methods (DFT) are accurate but scale steeply and reach only ~hundreds of atoms for picoseconds; classical force fields are fast but cannot break bonds or capture polarization. A neural network trained on DFT energies and forces — built with physical **equivariance** (respecting translation, rotation, permutation symmetry) and **locality** — interpolates the quantum energy surface at near-classical cost and can describe bond making/breaking. The critical limitation is **out-of-distribution failure**: encounter a configuration unlike the training data (a rare transition state, an unusual environment) and predictions can be silently, unphysically wrong. Generating sufficient, well-sampled quantum reference data — and validating extrapolation — is the real bottleneck, often addressed by active learning that adds new quantum calculations where the model is most uncertain.

atoms.title: Condensate biophysics: scaffolds, clients & material state
atoms.summary: Beyond simple phase separation, biomolecular condensates are tunable materials whose multivalent 'sticker–spacer' architecture sets composition, surface tension, and the liquid-to-gel-to-solid transitions that matter for function and disease.

depths.eli5: Cells make membraneless droplets that act like tiny liquid factories. The molecules inside have sticky spots connected by floppy linkers; how many sticky spots and how strong they are decides which droplets form, what they pull in, and whether they stay liquid or harden.
depths.core: Condensate-forming molecules follow a sticker–spacer logic: multivalent attractive motifs (stickers — aromatics, charged blocks, folded interaction domains) connected by flexible spacers. The number and strength of stickers, plus spacer solvent quality, set the saturation concentration for phase separation and tune which molecules are scaffolds (drive demixing) versus clients (partition in). The same polymer-network and surface-tension physics governing gels applies: condensates have interfacial tension, can wet surfaces, and can be viscoelastic rather than purely liquid.
depths.deep: The material state is a control variable, not a fixed property: condensates span liquid (fast internal rearrangement) to gel/glass (arrested) to amyloid-like solid, and physiological function or pathology depends on where a condensate sits and whether it ages over time. Aberrant liquid-to-solid maturation links condensates to neurodegeneration (e.g. FUS, TDP-43). Measuring this requires the right observables — FRAP for internal mobility, active microrheology for viscoelasticity, controlled in-vitro reconstitution to map phase diagrams — a clean instance of the field-wide lesson that you must match the measurement to the material property you care about, since 'is it a condensate?' is far less informative than 'what is its composition, dynamics, and material state?'

atoms.note: How many sticky spots ('stickers') and how strong they are set the phase diagram; a droplet's material state (liquid → gel → solid) is a tunable property that can drift with age, and pathological hardening links these droplets to disease. Match the measurement (FRAP, microrheology) to the question. ('FRAP' = bleach a spot and watch how fast fresh molecules flow back in, revealing how liquid it is; 'scaffold' drives the droplet, a 'client' just rides along inside.)

atoms.art_prompt: sticker-spacer chains with labeled multivalent sticky motifs coalescing into a droplet, a phase diagram with a saturation boundary, and a liquid-to-gel-to-solid material-state axis with an ageing arrow

quiz.prompt: In the sticker–spacer model of condensates, what roles do stickers and spacers play, and what distinguishes a scaffold from a client?
quiz.answer: Stickers are the multivalent attractive motifs that drive association; spacers are the flexible linkers connecting them and tuning solubility/solvent quality. Scaffolds are the components whose multivalent interactions drive phase separation; clients are molecules that partition into the condensate without driving its formation.

quiz.prompt: Why is a condensate's material state (liquid vs gel vs solid) considered a key, disease-relevant variable, and how would you measure it?
quiz.answer: Function often requires liquid-like fast exchange, while aberrant hardening (liquid-to-solid maturation/ageing) is linked to pathological aggregation in neurodegeneration. You measure internal dynamics by FRAP (recovery rate) and viscoelasticity by active microrheology, and map phase behavior by controlled in-vitro reconstitution — matching the observable to the material property.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Cells build many compartments *without membranes* by letting certain proteins and RNAs condense into droplets — but these are not just simple oil-in-water blobs. They are tunable **materials** with internal logic: some molecules act as the structural **scaffold** holding the droplet together, others as **clients** that partition in or out, and the whole thing can be liquid, gel, or solid depending on how its parts stick. Understanding *which* molecules condense, *what* gets in, and *how solid* it becomes is condensate biophysics.

### Precisely

**Biomolecular condensates** form by liquid–liquid phase separation, but their behaviour is governed by a **multivalent** "**sticker–spacer**" architecture: **stickers** are the cohesive interaction sites (aromatic residues, charged blocks, folded binding domains) and **spacers** are the flexible linkers between them. **Scaffolds** (high-valence molecules) drive demixing and set the network; **clients** (lower-valence) partition in by binding scaffolds. The number and strength of stickers tune **composition**, **surface tension**, and the **material state** — a liquid, a viscoelastic gel, or, pathologically, a solid.

### Worked example

A protein with many weak aromatic stickers spaced by disordered linkers phase-separates into a *liquid* droplet that rounds up and fuses. Add more or stronger stickers (or a disease mutation that increases sticker stickiness, or simply let it **age**) and the same condensate can undergo a **liquid-to-gel-to-solid transition** — flowing less, recovering more slowly after photobleaching, and eventually hardening into a structure that can seed **amyloid**. The sticker valence and strength thus dial the material from functional droplet to pathological aggregate.

### Why it's true / how it works

Multivalency creates a network of many weak crosslinks; the *density and lifetime* of those sticker–sticker bonds set the material's viscosity and elasticity (the same **gel/network** physics as polymer gels). Few, weak, fast-exchanging stickers give a liquid; many, strong, slow ones give a gel or solid. Composition is set by which clients can bind available scaffold stickers — a binding-affinity (**K_d**) bookkeeping at the droplet scale.

### Where it connects

It deepens **IDP/LLPS** phase separation into materials science, borrows **polymer-gel** network elasticity and **binding (K_d)** logic, and links aberrant maturation to **amyloid** disease — a major theme in neurodegeneration.

### Watch out

Not every condensate is a liquid, and "phase separation" is not automatically "functional" — material state matters, and aberrant **hardening** is often pathological. Demonstrating true LLPS (and its material state) requires showing liquid-like behaviour and its breakdown, not just observing a dense focus; over-attributing every cellular puncta to functional LLPS is a common overreach.

### Numbers & nuance

The **sticker–spacer** framework makes condensates *tunable materials*: sticker valence and affinity set the saturation concentration $c_{\text{sat}}$, the dense-phase concentration, the surface tension (which drives rounding and fusion), and the viscosity. **Scaffolds** (high-valence) drive demixing and define the network; **clients** (low-valence) partition in by binding scaffolds — explaining selective composition. Crucially, condensates can **age**: liquids can convert to viscoelastic gels and then solids as sticker contacts strengthen or become long-lived (driven by mutations, increased concentration, or time), and that hardening links aberrant condensates to **amyloid** pathology in ALS/FTD (FUS, TDP-43) and other diseases. The takeaway: "phase separation" alone is not function — the *material state* and its regulation are what matter, and not every cellular punctum is a functional liquid droplet.

atoms.title: Circular dichroism spectroscopy
atoms.summary: Chiral biomolecules absorb left- and right-circularly-polarized light differently; the far-UV spectrum is a quick fingerprint of secondary-structure content and folding.

depths.eli5: Proteins are 'handed,' so they twist left- and right-spinning light by different amounts. The pattern of that difference tells you roughly how much helix and sheet a protein has — and whether it's still folded.
depths.core: Circular dichroism (CD) measures the differential absorption of left- versus right-circularly-polarized light by chiral chromophores. In the far-UV (190–250 nm) the peptide backbone's amide transitions give signatures characteristic of secondary structure: α-helix shows a double minimum at 208 and 222 nm, β-sheet a single broader minimum near 218 nm, and random coil a minimum near 200 nm. Deconvolving a spectrum estimates the fractional helix/sheet/coil content, and watching the 222 nm signal versus temperature or denaturant gives a folding/melting curve.
depths.deep: CD is low-resolution but fast, low-sample, and works in solution — ideal for confirming a protein is folded, monitoring thermal/chemical denaturation to extract ΔG and T_m (tying back to two-state folding), and detecting conformational change on binding. Near-UV CD (250–320 nm) reports the tertiary environment of aromatic side chains, a sensitive (if hard-to-interpret) fingerprint of the native fold. Synchrotron-radiation CD extends the usable wavelength range for better deconvolution. It complements high-resolution methods: CD tells you fast whether a sample is worth taking to crystallography, NMR, or cryo-EM.

atoms.note: The 222 nm helix signal is the workhorse: track it as you heat or add denaturant to get a melting curve and ΔG. CD is the fast, low-sample 'is it folded, and how much helix vs sheet?' check before committing to expensive structural methods. ('Chiral' = handed, like a left vs right glove — proteins are chiral, so they treat left- and right-twisting light differently; 'far-UV' = short-wavelength ultraviolet, 190–250 nm.)

atoms.art_prompt: left- and right-circularly-polarized light absorbed differently by a chiral protein, a far-UV CD spectrum with the alpha-helix double minimum at 208 and 222 nm beside a beta-sheet single minimum

quiz.prompt: What does far-UV circular dichroism report about a protein, and what is the characteristic α-helix signature?
quiz.answer: It reports secondary-structure content (fractional helix/sheet/coil) from the backbone amide transitions. The α-helix gives a characteristic double minimum at 208 nm and 222 nm; β-sheet gives a single broader minimum near 218 nm.

quiz.prompt: How is CD used to measure protein stability?
quiz.answer: By monitoring a secondary-structure signal (commonly the helix band at 222 nm) as a function of temperature or denaturant, you obtain a cooperative melting curve; fitting it (often as two-state) yields the melting temperature T_m and the folding free energy ΔG.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Proteins are **chiral** — built from handed (left-handed) amino acids and twisted into handed helices and sheets — so they interact differently with left- versus right-twisting light. Measure that tiny difference in absorption across the ultraviolet and you get a quick fingerprint of how much helix and sheet a protein has, and whether it is folded at all — a fast, gentle health check that needs only a small amount of sample in solution.

### Precisely

**Circular dichroism (CD)** spectroscopy measures the difference in absorption of **left- and right-circularly-polarized light** by a chiral sample, as a function of wavelength. In the **far-UV** (~190–250 nm), the signal arises from the peptide backbone and reports **secondary-structure** content: an **α-helix** gives a characteristic spectrum with double minima near 208 and 222 nm; a **β-sheet** gives a single broader minimum near 218 nm; a random coil gives a strong minimum near 195 nm. Fitting a spectrum estimates the fractions of each structure.

### Worked example

Record a protein's far-UV CD and see deep negative bands at 208 and 222 nm — it is predominantly α-helical. Now heat the sample and re-measure: as it **unfolds**, the helical signature collapses toward a random-coil spectrum. Plotting the 222 nm signal versus temperature gives a **melting curve** whose sigmoidal midpoint is the melting temperature $T_m$ — exactly the **two-state folding** read-out, obtained quickly and non-destructively.

### Why it's true / how it works

Circularly polarized light has a handedness; a chiral chromophore (the regularly twisted backbone) absorbs the two handednesses unequally because the electronic transitions couple to the structure's geometry. Ordered secondary structures arrange the peptide bonds into regular, exciton-coupled arrays, producing their distinctive band shapes; disorder averages these out. So the spectral shape maps directly onto structural content.

### Where it connects

It rapidly quantifies the **secondary structure** of the **structure hierarchy**, monitors **two-state folding**/denaturation (melting curves, $\Delta G$), and complements high-resolution **Bragg**, **NMR**, and **cryo-EM** with a fast, low-resolution, solution-based assay.

### Watch out

CD gives **average secondary-structure content**, not *which* residues are in which structure, and the deconvolution into fractions is approximate (β-sheet estimates are especially unreliable). It needs accurate concentration and clean, non-absorbing buffers (chloride and many additives absorb in the far-UV and corrupt the spectrum).

### Numbers & nuance

Far-UV CD fingerprints: α-helix shows characteristic double minima near 208 and 222 nm plus a maximum near 192 nm; β-sheet a single minimum near 215–218 nm; random coil a strong minimum near 195 nm. Tracking the 222 nm signal versus temperature or denaturant gives a fast, non-destructive **melting curve** (the same two-state read-out, requiring only micrograms of protein). The method gives *average* secondary-structure content, **not** which residues adopt which structure, and β-sheet estimates are notoriously unreliable. It demands accurate concentration and far-UV-transparent buffers — chloride, many salts, and common additives absorb below ~200 nm and corrupt the spectrum. Near-UV CD (250–320 nm) separately reports tertiary structure via aromatic side-chain environments, a quick check that a protein is natively folded.

atoms.title: Patch clamp & single-channel recording
atoms.summary: A glass micropipette seals onto a patch of membrane to record the picoampere currents of individual ion channels — resolving single gating events that ensemble methods only average.

depths.eli5: Press a tiny glass tube tightly against a cell's surface and you can listen to a single ion channel clicking open and shut, counting the trickle of charge through one molecule at a time.
depths.core: Patch clamp forms a gigaohm-resistance seal between a fire-polished glass pipette and the cell membrane, electrically isolating a small patch so that the current through even a single channel (a few picoamperes) is measurable above noise. In voltage clamp the membrane voltage is held fixed and the current measured; single-channel records show discrete rectangular openings and closings, directly revealing the channel's unitary conductance, open probability, and dwell-time distributions. Configurations (cell-attached, whole-cell, inside-out, outside-out) expose either ensemble or single-molecule behavior and either side of the membrane to drugs.
depths.deep: Single-channel dwell-time histograms are a direct window onto the gating kinetics: the distribution of open and closed durations is a sum of exponentials whose number and rates reveal the underlying Markov-state gating scheme (connecting to ion-channel gating and Markov models). Averaging many single-channel records reproduces the macroscopic g_i(V) of the Hodgkin–Huxley description — making patch clamp the experimental bridge between molecular gating and whole-cell excitability. The technique (Neher and Sakmann, Nobel 1991) is the gold standard of electrophysiology and the readout for ion-channel drug screening.

atoms.note: How long a single channel stays open vs closed (its 'dwell times') reveals its Markov gating scheme; averaging many single channels rebuilds the smooth g(V) of Hodgkin–Huxley. Patch clamp is the molecular-to-cellular bridge in electrophysiology. ('Picoampere', pA, is a trillionth of an amp — the trickle through one channel; a 'gigaohm seal' is an extremely tight, high-resistance contact between glass and membrane.)

Wikipedia — Markov chain (the gating scheme it reveals)

atoms.art_prompt: a glass pipette forming a gigaohm seal on a membrane patch, a single-channel current trace showing rectangular open/closed events, and a dwell-time histogram fit by exponentials

quiz.prompt: What does patch clamp measure, and what makes recording a single channel possible?
quiz.answer: It measures the tiny (picoampere) ionic current through ion channels under voltage control. A gigaohm-resistance seal between the glass pipette and the membrane electrically isolates a small patch, lowering noise enough to resolve the current through a single channel as discrete open/closed events.

quiz.prompt: How do single-channel dwell-time distributions connect to a channel's gating model?
quiz.answer: The histograms of open and closed durations are sums of exponentials; the number of exponential components and their rate constants reveal the number of kinetic states and the transition rates of the channel's Markov gating scheme. Averaging many single-channel records reconstructs the macroscopic conductance g(V).

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Most measurements of ion flow average over millions of channels at once, smearing out the action. Patch clamp does something astonishing: it isolates a tiny patch of cell membrane — sometimes a *single* ion channel — and records the minuscule electrical current as that one channel flickers open and shut. You literally watch one protein molecule do its job, in real time, as discrete square steps of current.

### Precisely

**Patch clamp** presses a fire-polished glass micropipette against a cell membrane and applies gentle suction to form a high-resistance (gigaohm) **seal**. This electrically isolates the membrane patch so that the **picoampere** ($10^{-12}$ A) currents through individual **ion channels** can be measured while the voltage is held ("clamped") at a chosen value. Configurations include **cell-attached**, **whole-cell** (access to the whole cell's currents), **inside-out**, and **outside-out** patches, each exposing a different membrane face to the bath.

### Worked example

In a single-channel record, the current trace sits at zero (channel closed), then jumps to a fixed amplitude (channel open, passing a steady picoampere current), then drops back — a telegraph of square pulses. From many such events you measure the **single-channel conductance** (current/voltage), the **open probability**, and the **dwell-time distributions** that reveal the channel's gating kinetics — the rate constants of its conformational switching, invisible to ensemble methods that only see the average.

### Why it's true / how it works

The gigaohm seal is the key: it makes the patch's electrical resistance so high that the only meaningful current path is *through the channels in the patch*, so even single-molecule currents stand out above the noise. Clamping the voltage means any current measured is purely the ionic current at a known driving force (**Nernst/GHK** sets the channel's reversal potential), so conductance and gating can be read cleanly.

### Where it connects

Patch clamp provides the single-channel basis for the macroscopic conductances $g_i(V)$ of the **Hodgkin–Huxley** model, directly measures **ion-channel gating and selectivity**, uses the **Nernst/GHK** driving forces, and is the electrical analog of single-molecule optical methods like **smFRET**. It earned Neher and Sakmann the 1991 Nobel Prize.

### Watch out

Forming and maintaining the **gigaohm seal** is delicate; a leaky seal buries single-channel currents in noise. **Whole-cell** mode measures the *summed* current of all channels (not single events) and can dialyze (wash out) the cell's interior over time, altering the very signaling it measures — so the configuration must match the question.

### Numbers & nuance

The enabling trick is the **gigaohm (GΩ) seal** between glass pipette and membrane: its enormous resistance forces essentially all current through the channels in the patch, so even single-molecule **picoampere** currents stand out above noise. Single-channel records show square pulses whose amplitude gives the channel conductance (a few to ~100 pS), whose fraction-of-time-open gives the open probability, and whose **dwell-time distributions** reveal the gating rate constants — the kinetic detail ensemble methods only average away. Configurations trade off access: **whole-cell** measures the summed current of all channels but dialyzes the cytoplasm over time (washing out diffusible signaling molecules), while **excised** patches (inside-out/outside-out) give clean control of both membrane faces. Choosing the configuration to match the biological question is essential.

atoms.title: Single-molecule FRET conformational dynamics
atoms.summary: Watching FRET on one molecule at a time resolves conformational subpopulations, transition rates, and intermediates that ensemble averaging hides — a real-time movie of a single molecule's states.

depths.eli5: Ordinary FRET averages over billions of molecules, blurring different shapes together. Looking at one molecule at a time, you can actually watch it flip between conformations and time how long it stays in each — like following one dancer instead of a whole blurry crowd.
depths.core: Single-molecule FRET (smFRET) records the donor–acceptor transfer efficiency of individual molecules, either freely diffusing through a confocal spot (giving efficiency histograms whose peaks are distinct conformational states) or surface-immobilized and watched over time (giving trajectories that jump between FRET states). The distribution of dwell times in each state yields the transition rates between conformations directly — kinetics that bulk measurements only see as a relaxation average. It maps folding intermediates, IDP ensembles, motor stepping, and binding-induced conformational changes one molecule at a time.
depths.deep: smFRET trajectories are naturally analyzed as hidden Markov models / Markov state models: the observed noisy FRET signal is emitted by an underlying small set of discrete conformational states, and the inference recovers the states and their transition-rate matrix — the same formalism used to coarse-grain MD. Care is needed with the orientation factor κ² and photophysics (blinking, bleaching), and with distinguishing genuine states from shot noise. Combined with alternating-laser excitation and multi-color FRET, it dissects multistate machines; combined with force (in tweezers) it correlates conformation with mechanics. It is the experimental complement to MSM-analyzed simulation: both reduce complex dynamics to states-and-rates.

atoms.note: smFRET turns shape-changes into states-and-rates via hidden Markov / Markov-state analysis — the experimental mirror of coarse-graining a simulation. It resolves the subpopulations and dwell times that ordinary (bulk) FRET averages away. ('Ensemble' = measuring billions of molecules at once, which blurs them together; a 'hidden Markov model' infers the true hidden states behind a noisy signal.)

atoms.art_prompt: a single immobilized molecule's FRET-efficiency time trace hopping between two levels, a histogram with resolved subpopulation peaks, and a two-state kinetic scheme inferred by a hidden Markov model

quiz.prompt: What can single-molecule FRET resolve that ensemble FRET cannot?
quiz.answer: Distinct conformational subpopulations (as separate peaks/states rather than one averaged efficiency), real-time transitions between states, and the dwell-time distributions that give transition rates between conformations — all of which ensemble averaging washes into a single mean.

quiz.prompt: Why are smFRET trajectories analyzed with hidden Markov / Markov state models?
quiz.answer: The observed noisy FRET signal is treated as emitted by a small set of underlying discrete conformational states; HMM/MSM inference recovers those states and their transition-rate matrix from the time series — turning the trajectory into a states-and-rates description, the same coarse-graining used for molecular-dynamics data.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Ensemble experiments report an *average* over billions of molecules, so they blur together coexisting states and hide the moment-to-moment switching of any one molecule. Single-molecule FRET watches *one* molecule's two attached dyes report their separation continuously — so you see it jump between conformations in real time, count how many distinct states exist, and time the transitions directly. It is a movie of a single molecule's shape, not a blurred group photo.

### Precisely

**Single-molecule FRET (smFRET)** measures **FRET** efficiency (which encodes donor–acceptor distance via the $r^{-6}$ law) on **individual** labelled molecules, one at a time. Plotting the FRET efficiency over time for an immobilized molecule yields a trajectory that hops between discrete levels — each level a distinct **conformational state** — revealing **subpopulations**, **transition rates**, and short-lived **intermediates** that ensemble averaging conceals. A histogram of efficiencies from many molecules shows the populated states as separate peaks.

### Worked example

A protein that interconverts between an "open" (low FRET, dyes far apart) and "closed" (high FRET, dyes near) state appears in ensemble FRET as a single *average* efficiency — misleadingly suggesting one intermediate conformation. smFRET instead shows each molecule **dwelling** at low FRET, then abruptly jumping to high FRET and back. The dwell-time distributions give the opening and closing **rate constants** directly, and a rare third level might expose a transient intermediate no average could reveal.

### Why it's true / how it works

Because only one molecule is observed, its signal is not washed out by neighbours in other states. The steep distance dependence of FRET converts even small (ångström-scale) conformational motions into large, resolvable efficiency changes. Watching the *time order* of jumps (not just their populations) yields **kinetics** — the same information a **Markov state model** extracts from simulation, here measured experimentally.

### Where it connects

smFRET is the single-molecule application of **FRET**, measures the conformational **dynamics** that **NMR relaxation** and **Markov state models** also target, complements force-based single-molecule tools (**optical tweezers**, **AFM**), and resolves folding intermediates and motor/enzyme cycles.

### Watch out

Apparent distances inherit FRET's **orientation-factor** ($\kappa^2$) caveat and depend on accurate $R_0$. **Photophysics** — dye blinking and bleaching — can masquerade as conformational transitions, so artifacts must be excluded; and the molecule usually must be **immobilized or confined** long enough to watch, which can perturb the very dynamics being measured.

### Numbers & nuance

smFRET's power is resolving what ensembles average away: a protein flickering between an open (low-FRET) and closed (high-FRET) state shows up in bulk as one *misleading* intermediate efficiency, but single-molecule trajectories reveal discrete jumps whose dwell times give the forward/reverse **rate constants** directly — a real-time kinetic movie. Histograms of efficiency across many molecules expose distinct subpopulations and rare intermediates. Two practical hazards: dye **photophysics** (blinking, bleaching) can masquerade as conformational transitions and must be controlled, and the inferred distances inherit FRET's orientation-factor ($\kappa^2$) caveat, so smFRET is most trustworthy for *relative* state changes and rates. Molecules are usually immobilized (surface-tethered or in vesicles) to watch long enough — a constraint that can itself perturb the dynamics being measured.

atoms.title: Marcus theory of electron transfer
atoms.summary: Electron-transfer rate depends parabolically on driving force through a reorganization energy λ — predicting the counterintuitive 'inverted region' where more driving force slows the reaction.

depths.eli5: When an electron jumps between molecules, the surrounding atoms must rearrange to accommodate the new charges. The rate depends on how much driving force there is and how much rearrangement is needed — and surprisingly, too much driving force can actually slow the jump down.
depths.core: Marcus theory models electron transfer as a transition between two parabolic free-energy surfaces (reactant and product) along a nuclear reorganization coordinate. The activation free energy is ΔG‡ = (ΔG° + λ)²/(4λ), where λ is the reorganization energy — the cost of distorting the nuclei and solvent to the product geometry without transferring the electron. Plugging into an Eyring-like expression gives the rate. The rate is maximal when −ΔG° = λ (barrierless), and the famous inverted region appears when −ΔG° > λ: making the reaction more exergonic raises the barrier again, slowing it.
depths.deep: Combined with electronic coupling that decays exponentially with donor–acceptor distance, Marcus theory explains the ~14 Å spacing design rule of biological electron-transport chains: cofactors are placed so coupling keeps tunneling fast while the staircase of redox potentials (ΔG°) sits near the barrierless optimum. Proteins tune λ by controlling the dielectric/rigidity of the cofactor environment, lowering reorganization to speed physiological transfers. The inverted region — confirmed experimentally decades after prediction — is why charge recombination (very exergonic) can be slow, a feature photosynthesis exploits to prevent wasteful back-reactions.

atoms.note: Two knobs: the driving force ΔG° (how downhill the jump is) and the reorganization energy λ (how much the surroundings must rearrange). The rate is fastest when −ΔG° = λ; push past that and you enter the 'inverted region' where MORE driving force slows the jump — a trick photosynthesis uses to stop wasteful back-reactions. ('Electron transfer' = an electron hopping from a donor molecule to an acceptor; 'reorganization energy' = the cost of nudging the nuclei/solvent into the product's preferred arrangement.)

atoms.art_prompt: two parabolic free-energy surfaces crossing along a reorganization coordinate, the activation barrier shrinking to zero at -ΔG°=λ and re-growing in the inverted region

quiz.prompt: What is the reorganization energy λ in Marcus theory, and at what driving force is the electron-transfer rate maximal?
quiz.answer: λ is the free-energy cost of rearranging the nuclei and surrounding solvent from the reactant to the product geometry without moving the electron. The rate is maximal (barrierless) when the driving force exactly matches it: −ΔG° = λ.

quiz.prompt: What is the Marcus inverted region, and why does it occur?
quiz.answer: It is the regime where making a reaction more exergonic (−ΔG° > λ) actually slows electron transfer. From ΔG‡ = (ΔG° + λ)²/(4λ), the barrier is minimized at −ΔG° = λ; pushing −ΔG° beyond λ makes (ΔG° + λ)² grow again, re-raising the barrier and lowering the rate.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

When an electron jumps from a donor to an acceptor, the surrounding atoms and solvent — which had arranged themselves comfortably around the *old* charge distribution — must rearrange to suit the *new* one. That rearrangement costs energy, and it is the hidden bottleneck of electron transfer. Marcus theory's famous, counterintuitive prediction: pushing the reaction harder (more driving force) speeds it up only to a point — beyond an optimum, *more* driving force makes it *slower*. This is the "inverted region."

### Precisely

**Marcus theory** gives the electron-transfer rate as

$$k_{\text{ET}} \propto \exp\!\left[-\frac{(\Delta G^\circ + \lambda)^2}{4\lambda\,k_BT}\right],$$

where $\Delta G^\circ$ is the reaction's free-energy change (driving force, negative for favourable) and $\lambda$ is the **reorganization energy** — the energy to distort the nuclei/solvent from the reactant's equilibrium geometry to the product's *without* transferring the electron. The rate is **maximal** when $-\Delta G^\circ = \lambda$ (the activation barrier vanishes), and *decreases* on either side.

### Worked example

Hold $\lambda$ fixed and increase the driving force $-\Delta G^\circ$ from zero. At first the rate rises (the **normal region**). At $-\Delta G^\circ = \lambda$ the exponent is zero — the barrier disappears and the rate **peaks**. Push further, $-\Delta G^\circ > \lambda$, and the squared term grows again, so the rate **falls** — the **inverted region**. This non-monotonic behaviour, predicted in the 1950s and confirmed decades later, is why biological electron-transfer chains tune $\Delta G^\circ$ and $\lambda$ to sit near the optimum.

### Why it's true / how it works

Model the reactant and product as two parabolic free-energy wells along a nuclear "reorganization" coordinate, displaced vertically by $\Delta G^\circ$ and horizontally by an amount set by $\lambda$. Electron transfer happens where the parabolas cross (energy conservation). The crossing-point height — the activation barrier — works out to $(\Delta G^\circ+\lambda)^2/(4\lambda)$, giving the Gaussian rate law. The rate also falls off exponentially with donor–acceptor **distance** (electronic coupling).

### Where it connects

Marcus theory sets the *rates* of the steps whose *thermodynamics* the **redox potential** atom describes, governs the **electron transport chain** and photosynthesis, and is the electron-transfer analog of barrier-crossing **transition-state/Eyring** and **Kramers** theory. It won Marcus the 1992 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

### Watch out

The headline surprise is the **inverted region**: beyond the optimum, *increasing* driving force *slows* the reaction — the opposite of normal chemical intuition. Also, $\lambda$ (reorganization energy) is a property of the *environment's* response, not the molecules' internal bonds alone, so the same redox pair can transfer at very different rates in different surroundings.

### Numbers & nuance

The parabolic rate law peaks when $-\Delta G^\circ = \lambda$ (barrierless), then *decreases* for larger driving force — the famous **inverted region**, predicted in the 1950s and confirmed decades later (Nobel Prize 1992). Reorganization energy $\lambda$ has inner-sphere (bond rearrangement) and outer-sphere (solvent reorientation) parts, typically ~0.5–1.5 eV in biological electron transfer; it is a property of the *environment's* response, so the same redox pair transfers at very different rates in different surroundings. The rate also falls roughly exponentially with donor–acceptor **distance** (electronic coupling $\sim e^{-\beta r}$, $\beta\approx1.4$ Å⁻¹ through protein), which is why biological electron-transfer chains place cofactors ~10–14 Å apart — close enough for fast tunneling, far enough to control the path. Marcus theory sets the *rates*; redox potentials set the *thermodynamics*.

atoms.title: Verlet integration
atoms.summary: The time-reversible, symplectic stepping recipe MD uses to advance positions and velocities for millions of steps without slowly leaking energy.

depths.eli5: To make a movie of jiggling atoms you need a rule for drawing the next frame. Verlet's rule uses where each atom is, how fast it is going, and the push it feels right now to step forward a tiny bit — and it is built so the atoms do not secretly heat up or cool down over millions of frames.
depths.core: Velocity-Verlet advances position with r(t+Δt)=r+vΔt+½aΔt² and velocity with v(t+Δt)=v+½(a+a′)Δt, evaluating the force (acceleration) at both the old and the new position. It is time-reversible (run it backward and you retrace the path) and symplectic (it preserves phase-space volume), so the total energy oscillates within a bounded band for arbitrarily long runs instead of drifting off the way a naive forward-Euler step does.
depths.deep: A symplectic integrator does not conserve the true Hamiltonian exactly, but it exactly conserves a nearby 'shadow' Hamiltonian, which is why its energy error stays bounded rather than growing secularly. The local truncation error is O(Δt⁴) in position (global O(Δt²)); the timestep is capped by the fastest motion in the system — C–H bond stretches with ~10 fs periods force Δt≈1 fs unless those bonds are frozen by a constraint algorithm (SHAKE/LINCS), which then permits ~2 fs.

atoms.note: Symplectic ≈ 'volume-preserving in phase space.' That geometric property — not raw per-step accuracy — is what keeps a million-step trajectory from heating up or freezing. A formally more accurate but non-symplectic high-order Runge–Kutta step actually does worse over a long MD run.

Wikipedia — Euler method (the simpler step it beats)
Wikipedia — Molecular dynamics (where it is used)

atoms.art_prompt: an atom's path advancing as discrete arrow-steps along a smooth curve, beside a small energy gauge whose needle wobbles within a fixed band instead of drifting off-scale

quiz.prompt: Why does MD use the Verlet integrator instead of a simple forward-Euler step?
quiz.answer: Because Verlet is symplectic and time-reversible: it preserves phase-space volume and conserves a nearby 'shadow' energy, so the total energy stays within a bounded band over millions of steps. Forward Euler is neither, so its energy drifts steadily, ruining long simulations.

quiz.prompt: A simulation's fastest motion is C–H bond stretching with a period near 10 fs. Roughly what timestep can you use, and how do you make it larger?
quiz.answer: You need several steps per oscillation, so Δt ≈ 1 fs (about a tenth of the fastest period); larger makes the integrator unstable and the energy blow up. To reach ~2 fs you constrain (freeze) the X–H bonds with SHAKE or LINCS, removing the fastest motion so a bigger step stays stable.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A molecular-dynamics simulation is a flip-book of atomic positions. To draw the next page you need a stepping rule that turns the current positions, velocities, and forces into the positions a tiny instant later. The danger is that a careless rule slowly pumps energy in or out, so after a million steps the 'movie' is of a system at the wrong temperature. The Verlet family of integrators is built to avoid exactly that.

### Precisely

In the common **velocity-Verlet** form, with acceleration $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{F}/m$ from the force field,

$$\mathbf{r}_{t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{r}_t + \mathbf{v}_t\,\Delta t + \tfrac12\mathbf{a}_t\,\Delta t^2,\qquad \mathbf{v}_{t+\Delta t} = \mathbf{v}_t + \tfrac12\big(\mathbf{a}_t+\mathbf{a}_{t+\Delta t}\big)\Delta t.$$

The new velocity uses the force at **both** the old and the new positions. The scheme is **time-reversible** and **symplectic** (phase-space-volume preserving).

### Worked example

Suppose the fastest motion is a bond vibration of period $\sim 10\ \text{fs}$. Stable, accurate integration needs roughly ten steps per period, so $\Delta t \approx 1\ \text{fs}$. Freeze the stiff $\text{X-H}$ bonds with a constraint algorithm (SHAKE/LINCS) and the fastest remaining motion is slower, letting you double to $\Delta t \approx 2\ \text{fs}$ and simulate twice as long for the same cost.

### Why it's true / how it works

A symplectic integrator does not conserve the exact energy, but it **exactly conserves a nearby 'shadow' Hamiltonian**. Because that shadow energy differs from the true energy by a small bounded amount, the true energy can only *oscillate* within a band — it cannot drift away over time. This is the geometric reason a 'less accurate' symplectic step beats a 'more accurate' non-symplectic one for long runs.

### Where it connects

It is the engine inside **molecular dynamics**; the same idea underlies Langevin/Brownian-dynamics integrators (Verlet plus a friction-and-noise term) and any long-time Hamiltonian simulation in physics.

### Watch out

The timestep is dictated by the **fastest** degree of freedom, not the one you care about. Push $\Delta t$ too high and the integrator becomes unstable and the energy explodes. The cure is to *remove* fast motions (bond constraints, hydrogen-mass repartitioning), not to use a fancier non-symplectic integrator.

### Numbers & nuance

Global accuracy is only $O(\Delta t^2)$, yet velocity-Verlet dominates MD precisely because of its **long-time stability**, not its order. Typical timesteps: $1\ \text{fs}$ unconstrained, $2\ \text{fs}$ with $\text{X-H}$ constraints, up to $\sim 4\ \text{fs}$ with hydrogen-mass repartitioning — each trick works by slowing the fastest motion so the same symplectic step stays stable.

atoms.title: Root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF)
atoms.summary: Each atom's wobble amplitude over a trajectory — the simulation's read-out of local flexibility, and the bridge to crystallographic B-factors.

depths.eli5: Watch one atom in the movie and measure how far it usually strays from its own average spot — that is its RMSF. Floppy loops have a big RMSF; the rigid core barely moves, so its RMSF is small.
depths.core: For atom i, RMSF_i is the root-mean-square distance of its position from its own time-averaged position over the trajectory. Plotted against residue number it is a flexibility fingerprint: peaks at loops, chain termini, and hinges; valleys in the packed core and in secondary-structure elements. It maps onto experiment through the crystallographic B-factor (Debye–Waller factor), B_i=(8π²/3)⟨Δr_i²⟩, so RMSF² is proportional to B.
depths.deep: RMSF is not RMSD. RMSD measures how far an entire structure has moved from a reference — one number per frame, after removing overall translation and rotation. RMSF measures each atom's spread about its own mean — one number per atom, after the same alignment. Comparing simulated RMSF to experimental B-factors is a standard sanity check on a trajectory, but B-factors also absorb crystal disorder, lattice contacts, and refinement choices, so the agreement is qualitative, not exact.

atoms.note: Align first. RMSF (and RMSD) only mean what you expect after you remove the molecule's overall tumbling and drift by a rigid-body superposition — otherwise a perfectly rigid protein that is merely rotating looks 'flexible.'

resources.label: Wikipedia — Root-mean-square deviation of atomic positions
Wikipedia — Molecular dynamics (the trajectory it analyzes)

atoms.art_prompt: a protein backbone colored from blue still core to red wagging loops and floppy tails, with a translucent cloud around each residue sized by its wobble amplitude

quiz.prompt: What does the RMSF of an atom measure, and which parts of a protein have high RMSF?
quiz.answer: It measures how much that atom fluctuates around its own time-averaged position over the trajectory (root-mean-square). Loops, chain termini, and hinge regions have high RMSF; the tightly packed hydrophobic core and rigid secondary structure have low RMSF.

quiz.prompt: Simulated RMSF and experimental B-factors are related by B=(8π²/3)⟨Δr²⟩. A residue has RMSF = 1.0 Å. What is its isotropic B-factor?
quiz.answer: ⟨Δr²⟩ = RMSF² = 1.0 Å², so B = (8π²/3)(1.0) ≈ 26.3 Å² (since 8π²/3 ≈ 26.3). A 1.0 Å fluctuation corresponds to a B-factor of about 26 Å².

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Once you have an MD trajectory — a movie of the molecule jiggling — you want a single number per atom that says 'how much does this part move?' That number is the root-mean-square fluctuation. It turns a long, noisy trajectory into a clean flexibility map you can color onto the structure.

### Precisely

For atom $i$ with instantaneous position $\mathbf{r}_i(t)$ and time-average $\langle\mathbf{r}_i\rangle$,

$$\mathrm{RMSF}_i = \sqrt{\big\langle (\mathbf{r}_i - \langle\mathbf{r}_i\rangle)^2\big\rangle},$$

the average taken over the (superposed) frames. Plotted versus residue number it peaks at loops, termini, and hinges and dips in the core.

### Worked example

Crystallographers report a **B-factor** (temperature factor) per atom, related to its mean-square displacement by $B=\tfrac{8\pi^2}{3}\langle\Delta r^2\rangle$. So a residue with $\mathrm{RMSF}=1.0\ \text{Å}$ predicts $B=\tfrac{8\pi^2}{3}(1.0)\approx 26\ \text{Å}^2$. Comparing your simulated RMSF profile to the experimental B-factor profile is a quick reality check on the simulation.

### Why it's true / how it works

RMSF is just the **standard deviation of an atom's position** in 3-D. Because thermal motion is (to first order) harmonic about each atom's mean, the spread of positions is Gaussian and its width — the RMSF — is the natural single-number summary, which is exactly the quantity X-ray refinement encodes in the B-factor.

### Where it connects

It is computed from a **molecular-dynamics** trajectory, validated against **crystallographic** B-factors, and complements **RMSD** (global drift) and normal-mode/elastic-network pictures of flexibility.

### Watch out

Two traps. First, **align the frames** (remove overall translation/rotation) or rigid-body tumbling fakes flexibility. Second, **RMSF is per-atom; RMSD is per-frame** — they answer different questions and are easy to confuse.

### Numbers & nuance

The RMSF–B-factor map runs both ways but only qualitatively: experimental B-factors also soak up crystal-lattice disorder, static heterogeneity, and refinement modeling, so simulated and measured profiles should *track* each other, not match digit-for-digit. The conversion constant is $\tfrac{8\pi^2}{3}\approx 26.3$, so an RMSF of $0.5\ \text{Å}$ is $B\approx 6.6\ \text{Å}^2$ (rigid) and $1.5\ \text{Å}$ is $B\approx 59\ \text{Å}^2$ (very floppy).

atoms.title: Replica-exchange (parallel tempering)
atoms.summary: Run many copies at a ladder of temperatures and swap them by a Metropolis rule, so the barrier-crossing freedom of the hot copies flows down to give correct, fast sampling at the cold one.

depths.eli5: One simulation can get stuck in a valley. So run several at once — some hot, some cold. The hot copies leap over hills easily; every so often you let a hot copy and a cold copy trade places. That hands the freedom to explore down to the cold copy you actually care about.
depths.core: Replica-exchange MD (parallel tempering) simulates M non-interacting copies at temperatures T_1<T_2<...<T_M. Periodically it attempts to exchange the configurations of two neighboring replicas, accepting with probability min(1, exp[(β_i−β_j)(U_i−U_j)]), where β=1/k_BT. High-temperature replicas cross energy barriers readily; the swaps carry that mobility down the ladder so the lowest-temperature replica samples its Boltzmann distribution far faster than a single run could, while detailed balance guarantees each temperature keeps its correct ensemble.
depths.deep: Swap acceptance depends on the overlap of neighboring replicas' potential-energy distributions; to hold acceptance near 20–40% the temperatures are spaced roughly geometrically. Because energy fluctuations scale as √(degrees of freedom), the number of replicas needed to span a temperature range grows as √N — the method's Achilles heel for large explicit-solvent systems. Variants such as Hamiltonian replica exchange and replica-exchange-with-solute-tempering (REST) scale only the interactions that matter, dodging the √N cost.

atoms.note: Detailed balance is the safety net: the Metropolis swap rule is constructed so that, despite the trading, every replica still samples the exact Boltzmann distribution for its own temperature. You get faster sampling without biasing the result.

resources.label: Wikipedia — Boltzmann distribution (what each replica samples)
Wikipedia — Simulated annealing (the contrast: one cooling run)
Wikipedia — Molecular dynamics (the engine per replica)

atoms.art_prompt: a vertical ladder of identical simulation boxes shading from cold blue at the bottom to hot red at the top, with curved swap arrows trading contents between adjacent rungs

quiz.prompt: In replica-exchange MD, what is being run, and what gets exchanged?
quiz.answer: Many independent copies (replicas) of the system run in parallel at a ladder of increasing temperatures, and periodically the configurations of two neighboring-temperature replicas are swapped, accepted by a Metropolis rule. The high-temperature replicas cross barriers and feed that exploration down to the low-temperature replica.

quiz.prompt: Why are the replica temperatures spaced geometrically rather than evenly, and what limits how large a system you can treat this way?
quiz.answer: Swaps are only accepted when neighboring replicas' energy distributions overlap; geometric spacing keeps that overlap (and the ~20–40% acceptance) roughly uniform up the ladder. Because energy fluctuations grow as √(degrees of freedom), the number of replicas needed scales as √N, so large explicit-solvent systems demand prohibitively many replicas.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A single simulation at body temperature can fall into one deep energy valley — say one folded shape — and never climb out to see the alternatives in any reachable amount of compute. Heat a copy up and it sails over those hills, but a hot copy samples the wrong (too-disordered) distribution. Replica exchange marries the two: keep a cold copy for the right answer and a hot copy for the mobility, and periodically let them trade places.

### Precisely

Run $M$ replicas at $T_1<T_2<\dots<T_M$. Every so often, propose swapping the configurations of an adjacent pair $(i,j)$ and accept with

$$P_{\text{swap}} = \min\!\big(1,\ e^{(\beta_i-\beta_j)(U_i-U_j)}\big),\qquad \beta=\tfrac{1}{k_BT}.$$

This is a Metropolis rule on the *joint* ensemble, so detailed balance holds and every replica keeps sampling its own Boltzmann distribution.

### Worked example

A peptide that interconverts between two folds too slowly to see in one trajectory: stack ~16 replicas from 300 K to ~450 K. The 450 K replica hops between folds in nanoseconds; each accepted swap shuttles one of those well-mixed configurations downward, so the 300 K replica accumulates both folds in their correct ratio far sooner than a plain 300 K run would.

### Why it's true / how it works

The swap is just a Monte-Carlo move in an enlarged space whose stationary distribution is the **product** of each replica's Boltzmann distribution. Because the move satisfies detailed balance, it cannot distort any single-temperature ensemble — it only speeds up how quickly each one is explored.

### Where it connects

It sits beside **molecular dynamics** (the per-replica engine), **Monte-Carlo / Metropolis** sampling (the swap rule), the **Boltzmann distribution** (what is preserved), and other enhanced-sampling methods (umbrella sampling, metadynamics) that attack the same rare-event problem differently.

### Watch out

Swaps only happen if neighboring replicas' **energy histograms overlap**. Too few replicas → no accepted swaps → you have just run several independent simulations for nothing. The cost scales as $\sqrt{N}$ replicas, which is brutal for big solvated systems — hence solute-only variants (REST).

### Numbers & nuance

Practitioners tune the ladder for ~20–40% swap acceptance, which for atomistic systems means geometric temperature spacing and a replica count that grows as $\sqrt{N}$. That $\sqrt{N}$ scaling is why Hamiltonian replica exchange and REST — which temper only the solute or a chosen subset of interactions — are preferred for large explicit-solvent simulations.

atoms.title: Coarse-graining
atoms.summary: Lump groups of atoms into single beads and replace their detailed forces with a potential of mean force — buying length and time scales at the cost of chemical detail.

depths.eli5: Instead of tracking every atom, bundle a few together into one 'bead' — like drawing a person as a stick figure instead of every cell. Fewer pieces and smoother motion let you simulate much bigger things for much longer, but you lose the fine detail.
depths.core: A coarse-grained model maps several atoms onto one interaction site (for example MARTINI lumps roughly four heavy atoms per bead) and replaces the atomistic forces with effective interactions. The correct effective potential is the potential of mean force: the free energy left after integrating out the eliminated degrees of freedom. Fewer particles, a smoother energy landscape, and the loss of fast bond vibrations let you take bigger timesteps and reach micro- to milliseconds and large assemblies — at the price of lost chemistry and softened entropy.
depths.deep: Because the CG potential is a free energy, it is state-point dependent: a model parameterized at one temperature or concentration is not guaranteed to transfer to another (the representability and transferability problems). Smoothing the landscape also accelerates dynamics non-uniformly, so coarse-grained time is not physical time and kinetics must be reinterpreted (e.g. via a friction rescaling). Systematic 'bottom-up' methods — iterative Boltzmann inversion, force matching, relative-entropy minimization — try to recover the true PMF, whereas 'top-down' models like MARTINI instead fit experimental thermodynamics.

atoms.note: The coarse-grained potential is a free energy, not a mechanical energy — that is the whole subtlety. Because free energies depend on temperature and concentration, a CG model tuned at one condition can quietly fail at another, and the sped-up dynamics no longer tell physical time.
