Wikipedia — Martini force field (a top-down CG model)
Wikipedia — Free energy (what the bead potential is)
Wikipedia — Molecular dynamics (the simulation it accelerates)

atoms.art_prompt: an all-atom protein on the left dissolving into a handful of large smooth beads on the right, with a clock and a ruler showing the longer times and bigger sizes it unlocks

quiz.prompt: In coarse-graining, what replaces the detailed atomic forces between beads, and what do you gain?
quiz.answer: The effective interaction is the potential of mean force — the free energy remaining after averaging over (integrating out) the atomic degrees of freedom you removed. You gain access to much larger systems and longer timescales, because there are fewer particles, a smoother landscape, and no fast bond vibrations capping the timestep.

quiz.prompt: Name one thing you lose or must be careful about when you coarse-grain a system.
quiz.answer: Any of: lost chemical/atomic detail; the CG potential is a free energy, so it is temperature- and concentration-dependent and may not transfer between conditions; the dynamics are artificially accelerated, so simulated time is not physical time; entropy is softened. Coarse-grained kinetics in particular must be reinterpreted.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Most questions about a membrane or a protein assembly do not need every hydrogen. Coarse-graining throws away that fine detail on purpose: it groups several atoms into one fat 'bead' and gives the beads simple effective interactions. With far fewer particles and no fast vibrations, the simulation reaches sizes and times — whole vesicles, milliseconds — that all-atom MD cannot touch.

### Precisely

Define a mapping $\mathbf{M}$ from atomic coordinates $\mathbf{r}$ to bead coordinates $\mathbf{R}$. The exact effective potential reproducing the bead-level structure is the **potential of mean force**

$$U_{\text{CG}}(\mathbf{R}) = -k_BT\,\ln\!\int e^{-U(\mathbf{r})/k_BT}\,\delta\big(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{r})\big)\,d\mathbf{r},$$

i.e. the **free energy** after integrating out everything the mapping discards. It is an average over the hidden atomic detail, not a mechanical bond energy.

### Worked example

MARTINI maps about four heavy atoms to one bead. A lipid becomes ~12 beads instead of ~50 atoms; with the smoother landscape the timestep rises and the effective speed-up is often quoted as ~$10^3\times$ or more — enough to watch a lipid bilayer self-assemble or a protein insert into a membrane.

### Why it's true / how it works

Integrating out degrees of freedom always produces a **free energy**, because you are summing $e^{-U/k_BT}$ over the eliminated coordinates. That is why the bead potential carries entropy from the hidden atoms — and why it inherits a temperature and concentration dependence that a true mechanical potential would not have.

### Where it connects

It rests on **free energy** and the **potential of mean force**, runs through **molecular dynamics**, and is the route to mesoscale phenomena — membrane shapes (Helfrich elasticity), polymer melts, and large macromolecular assemblies — that atomistic detail cannot reach.

### Watch out

The CG potential is a free energy, so it is **state-point dependent**: a model tuned at 300 K and one salt concentration may misbehave elsewhere (transferability). And because the landscape is smoothed, **dynamics are sped up unevenly** — coarse-grained 'time' is not physical time, so rate comparisons need a friction rescaling.

### Numbers & nuance

There are two philosophies. **Bottom-up** methods (iterative Boltzmann inversion, force matching, relative-entropy minimization) try to reproduce the true PMF from atomistic reference data; **top-down** models (MARTINI) instead fit experimental partitioning free energies and densities. Each trades a different kind of accuracy: bottom-up is structurally faithful at its reference state but poorly transferable; top-down is robust across systems but coarser about any single one.

atoms.title: Flory scaling (real chains in solvent)
atoms.summary: A real polymer swells beyond the ideal random-walk size because its own segments cannot overlap; balancing that excluded-volume repulsion against entropic elasticity gives R ~ N^(3/5) in good solvent.

depths.eli5: An ideal chain is allowed to walk back through itself, like a ghost. A real chain is made of atoms that take up space, so it has to puff out a bit to avoid crowding itself. Flory worked out exactly how much puffier it gets: a real chain in a friendly solvent is fatter than the ghost version, and he predicted the exact swelling with a one-line energy argument.
depths.core: An ideal chain of N segments of length b has size R0 ~ b·N^(1/2). Real segments cannot occupy the same space (excluded volume), so in a 'good' solvent the chain swells. Flory estimated the free energy as a sum of an entropic-elastic term that resists stretching, F_el/k_BT ~ R^2/(N b^2), and a repulsive excluded-volume term from segment-segment contacts, F_rep/k_BT ~ v N^2/R^3 (in 3D), where v is the excluded volume per segment. Minimizing the sum over R gives R ~ v^(1/5) b^(2/5) N^(3/5): the Flory exponent v = 3/5 in three dimensions, larger than the ideal 1/2.
depths.deep: The general-dimension result of the same balance is nu = 3/(d+2), giving 3/4 in 2D, 3/5 in 3D, and 1/2 (ideal) at the upper critical dimension d=4. The 3D value is famously close to the exact renormalization-group value nu ~ 0.588 - Flory's success is partly a cancellation of two errors (he overestimates both the repulsion and the elasticity). Solvent quality tunes the regime: in a good solvent v>0 and the chain is swollen (nu=3/5); at the theta temperature the effective two-body term vanishes and the chain is nearly ideal (nu=1/2); in a poor solvent v<0 and the chain collapses into a dense globule, R ~ N^(1/3). The swollen-to-globule change is the coil-globule transition, the toy model for the entropic side of protein folding.

atoms.note: nu = 1/2 is the ghost (ideal) chain, nu = 3/5 is the self-avoiding chain in good solvent, nu = 1/3 is the collapsed globule. Reading a measured size exponent off a log-log plot of R vs N immediately tells you which solvent regime a polymer is in.
sources: Wikipedia (ideal chain; Flory theory; self-avoiding walk)

resources.label: Wikipedia - Self-avoiding walk (the nu~3/5 real chain)

atoms.art_prompt: two polymer coils side by side over a faint log-log grid: a compact translucent 'ghost' coil labeled N^(1/2) and a visibly puffier self-avoiding coil labeled N^(3/5), with little repulsion arrows pushing segments apart in the second

quiz.prompt: What is the Flory exponent nu for a flexible polymer in a good solvent, in a theta solvent, and in a poor solvent?
quiz.answer: Good solvent: nu = 3/5 (swollen, self-avoiding). Theta solvent: nu = 1/2 (effectively ideal, excluded volume cancelled). Poor solvent: nu = 1/3 (collapsed globule). Size scales as R ~ b·N^nu in all three.

quiz.prompt: Flory writes the chain free energy as F/k_BT ~ R^2/(Nb^2) + vN^2/R^3 in 3D. Minimize it to show R ~ N^(3/5).
quiz.answer: Differentiate with respect to R and set to zero: 2R/(Nb^2) - 3vN^2/R^4 = 0, so R^5 ~ v N^3 b^2, giving R ~ v^(1/5) b^(2/5) N^(3/5). The elastic term wants R small, the repulsion wants R large; their balance fixes the exponent nu = 3/5. (The general-d balance R^(d+2) ~ vN^3 b^2 gives nu = 3/(d+2).)

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

The **ideal chain** treats a polymer as a random walk that is allowed to pass through itself - a ghost. Real chains are made of atoms that take up room, so a chain cannot fold back onto its own segments. That self-avoidance pushes the coil open, making it bigger than the ideal $N^{1/2}$ prediction. Flory's genius was to capture exactly how much bigger with a single back-of-envelope energy balance.

### Precisely

Write the free energy of a coil of size $R$ as two competing pieces:

$$\frac{F}{k_BT} \;\sim\; \underbrace{\frac{R^2}{N b^2}}_{\text{entropic elasticity (resists stretching)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{v\,N^2}{R^3}}_{\text{excluded-volume repulsion (resists crowding)}}.$$

The first term is the entropic-elastic cost of holding the chain out to size $R$; the second counts the $\sim N^2/R^3$ pairwise contacts, each costing an excluded volume $v$. Minimizing over $R$:

$$R \sim v^{1/5} b^{2/5} N^{3/5}, \qquad \nu = \tfrac{3}{5}.$$

### Worked example

Double the length of a chain in good solvent, $N\to 2N$. An ideal chain would grow by $2^{1/2}\approx1.41\times$; a real chain grows by $2^{3/5}\approx1.52\times$. The self-avoiding chain swells faster - measurable directly by light or neutron scattering as a steeper slope on a $\log R$ vs $\log N$ plot.

### Why it's true / how it works

Neither term alone has a minimum: elasticity alone collapses the chain, repulsion alone explodes it. The *competition* picks a unique size, and the power that survives the algebra is the universal exponent - independent of the chemical details buried in $b$ and $v$.

### Where it connects

It sits directly on top of the **ideal chain** ($\nu=1/2$) and **entropic elasticity** (the $R^2/Nb^2$ spring), and it underlies the **worm-like chain**, polymer-solution thermodynamics, and the coil-globule collapse that is a toy model for protein folding.

### Watch out

The exponent depends on **solvent quality**. Good solvent $\Rightarrow v>0\Rightarrow \nu=3/5$. At the *theta* temperature the effective two-body repulsion vanishes ($v=0$) and the chain is nearly ideal, $\nu=1/2$. In a poor solvent $v<0$ and the chain collapses, $R\sim N^{1/3}$.

### Numbers & nuance

Flory's $\nu=3/5=0.600$ is uncannily close to the exact renormalization-group value $\nu\approx0.588$ - a near-miss cancellation of two opposite errors. The general dimension formula $\nu=3/(d+2)$ even gives the right ideal limit at the upper critical dimension $d=4$.

atoms.title: Rouse model (chain dynamics)
atoms.summary: Treat a polymer as beads joined by entropic springs, each bead obeying a Langevin equation with independent drag - the simplest dynamics of a chain, giving a longest relaxation time that grows as N^2 and monomer motion that subdiffuses as t^(1/2).

depths.eli5: Picture a chain as beads connected by tiny springs, each bead jiggled by the surrounding fluid and dragged by it. The Rouse model is the simplest way to ask 'how fast does a floppy chain wiggle and rearrange?' Its answer: a single bead at first wanders strangely slowly (it is tied to its neighbors), and the whole chain takes a time that grows like the square of its length to forget its shape.
depths.core: The Rouse model couples the ideal chain's entropic springs to Langevin dynamics. Each of the N beads feels (i) spring forces from its two neighbors, with spring constant 3k_BT/b^2, (ii) a local friction -zeta(dr/dt), and (iii) independent thermal noise. Diagonalizing the connectivity into normal (Rouse) modes p = 1..N-1, each mode relaxes exponentially with tau_p = tau_R/p^2, so the longest mode tau_R = zeta N^2 b^2/(3 pi^2 k_BT) sets the time to relax the whole chain. The center of mass diffuses with D = k_BT/(N zeta), proportional to 1/N, and a tagged monomer subdiffuses, <dr^2> ~ t^(1/2), until t ~ tau_R, after which it crosses over to ordinary diffusion.
depths.deep: The crucial omissions are excluded volume and hydrodynamic interactions: beads pass through each other and the solvent does not transmit backflow from one bead to another. That makes Rouse the correct picture for unentangled polymer MELTS, where surrounding chains screen both effects - there it predicts viscosity eta proportional to N and the t^(1/2) monomer subdiffusion seen by neutron spin-echo. In dilute SOLUTION, hydrodynamics matters and the Zimm model (tau ~ N^(3nu), monomer t^(2/3)) replaces it. Above the entanglement length the chain is confined to a tube and reptation (tau ~ N^3) takes over. So Rouse is the unentangled baseline from which the harder theories branch.

atoms.note: Two numbers are the Rouse signature: the longest relaxation time scales as N^2 (each mode tau_p = tau_R/p^2) and a single monomer subdiffuses as t^(1/2), slower than free diffusion because it is tethered to the rest of the chain.
sources: Doi & Edwards, Theory of Polymer Dynamics - concepts only

resources.label: Wikipedia - Reptation (what takes over when entangled)

atoms.art_prompt: a beads-on-springs chain floating in a stippled solvent, with one tagged bead tracing a slow tangled subdiffusive path labeled t^(1/2), and a faint set of standing-wave Rouse modes p=1,2,3 sketched beneath it

quiz.prompt: What does the Rouse model represent a polymer as, and what does it deliberately ignore?
quiz.answer: Beads connected by entropic springs, each bead obeying a Langevin equation (local drag + thermal noise). It ignores excluded volume (beads can overlap) and hydrodynamic interactions (no solvent backflow between beads), which makes it the right model for unentangled melts rather than dilute solutions.

quiz.prompt: Rouse mode p relaxes with tau_p = tau_R/p^2. If the longest relaxation time of a chain is 1 microsecond, roughly how fast does the p=4 internal mode relax, and what does that mode physically represent?
quiz.answer: tau_4 = tau_R/4^2 = 1 us / 16 ~ 63 ns. Higher-p modes relax faster as 1/p^2 because they describe shorter sub-sections of the chain (mode p involves ~N/p beads); small-scale wiggles equilibrate quickly while the whole-chain shape (p=1) takes the full tau_R.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

The **ideal chain** tells you a polymer's *shape* statistics but says nothing about *motion*. The Rouse model is the simplest way to set that chain moving: keep the entropic springs that hold neighboring beads together, drop each bead into a **Langevin** bath of drag plus random kicks, and ask how fast the chain wiggles and forgets its conformation.

### Precisely

Bead $n$ obeys

$$\zeta\frac{d\mathbf{r}_n}{dt} = k\,(\mathbf{r}_{n+1}-2\mathbf{r}_n+\mathbf{r}_{n-1}) + \boldsymbol{\xi}_n(t),\qquad k=\frac{3k_BT}{b^2}.$$

Diagonalizing the connectivity gives independent **Rouse modes** $p$, each an exponential relaxation with

$$\tau_p = \frac{\tau_R}{p^2},\qquad \tau_R \sim \frac{\zeta N^2 b^2}{3\pi^2 k_BT}.$$

The center of mass diffuses with $D = k_BT/(N\zeta)\propto 1/N$, and a single monomer subdiffuses, $\langle\Delta r^2\rangle\sim t^{1/2}$, until $t\approx\tau_R$.

### Worked example

Double the chain length. The longest relaxation time grows by $2^2=4\times$ and the center-of-mass diffusion halves ($D\propto 1/N$). A neutron spin-echo experiment on a melt sees the tagged-monomer mean-square displacement rise as $t^{1/2}$ - the fingerprint that distinguishes a connected chain from free Brownian beads (which would give $t^1$).

### Why it's true / how it works

The springs couple neighbors, so a bead cannot move freely - it must drag its neighbors along. Mathematically the coupling diagonalizes into standing-wave modes; the slowest (whole-chain) mode controls relaxation and scales as $N^2$ because the restoring force per mode weakens as the chain lengthens while the friction it must move grows.

### Where it connects

It is **Langevin dynamics** applied to the **ideal chain**. Add hydrodynamic backflow and you get the **Zimm model** (dilute solution); add entanglements and you get reptation; coarse-grain further and you reach the rheology of polymer melts.

### Watch out

Rouse has no excluded volume and no hydrodynamics, so it is *wrong* for a single chain in dilute solution - there the solvent carries momentum from bead to bead and Zimm dynamics ($\tau\sim N^{3\nu}$, monomer $t^{2/3}$) win. Rouse is right for **unentangled melts**, where neighboring chains screen both effects.

### Numbers & nuance

The Rouse melt viscosity grows only linearly, $\eta\propto N$, until chains get long enough to entangle; above that the experimental viscosity jumps to $\eta\propto N^{3.4}$ and you have crossed from Rouse into reptation.

atoms.title: Equipartition theorem
atoms.summary: At thermal equilibrium every quadratic degree of freedom carries an average energy of ½k_BT — the universal currency of thermal motion.

depths.eli5: Heat is just jiggling, and thermodynamics shares the jiggling out fairly. Every independent way a thing can store motion-energy — sliding left-right, spinning, stretching like a spring — gets the same average ration: about half of a tiny fixed amount called k_BT. That single number (roughly 0.6 kcal per mole at body temperature) is the size of one 'kick' of thermal energy, and it sets how fast molecules rattle around.
depths.core: The equipartition theorem says that, in classical thermal equilibrium, each degree of freedom that appears as a quadratic term in the energy (½mv² for a velocity component, ½kx² for a spring coordinate) holds an average energy of exactly ½k_BT. A free atom has three translational degrees of freedom, so its average kinetic energy is (3/2)k_BT; this fixes the thermal speed of molecules and the energy scale of Brownian motion. A harmonic bond has two quadratic terms (kinetic + potential), so it averages k_BT. The theorem is what makes k_BT 'the' energy unit of biophysics: bond fluctuations, the stretch of DNA under thermal forces, and the diffusive kicks in the Langevin equation are all measured in units of k_BT.
depths.deep: Equipartition is a *classical* result and fails when quantum spacing matters. A degree of freedom is 'frozen out' and stops absorbing ½k_BT once its energy-level spacing ħω exceeds k_BT — which is why molecular vibrations (stiff, high ω) contribute little at room temperature while translations and rotations (soft) are fully active, and why the heat capacity of solids drops below the Dulong–Petit value 3R as temperature falls. Equipartition is the classical limit of the full quantum statistical-mechanical average.

Wikipedia — Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution (the speeds it sets)
LibreTexts Chemistry — Physical & Theoretical Chemistry texts

atoms.art_prompt: a molecule with arrows for sliding, spinning, and a stretching spring, each labeled with an equal energy bucket of one-half k_B T

quiz.prompt: How much average energy does a single quadratic degree of freedom carry at thermal equilibrium?
quiz.answer: ½k_BT — half of k_BT per quadratic degree of freedom.

quiz.prompt: Use equipartition to find the average kinetic energy of a free molecule and its molar heat capacity, then explain why a stiff covalent bond's vibration contributes far less than ½k_BT at 300 K.
quiz.answer: A free molecule has 3 translational (quadratic kinetic) degrees of freedom, so ⟨KE⟩ = 3 × ½k_BT = (3/2)k_BT; for a mole U = (3/2)RT and C_V = (3/2)R ≈ 12.5 J/mol/K (the monatomic-gas value). A vibration adds 2 quadratic terms (kinetic + potential) → k_BT each when active, but equipartition is classical: a degree of freedom only absorbs its full share when its quantum spacing ħω ≲ k_BT. A stiff bond has ħω ≫ k_BT at 300 K, so it is 'frozen out' and stores almost no thermal energy — the same reason solids fall below the Dulong–Petit 3R heat capacity as they cool.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Temperature is a measure of jiggling, and equilibrium shares the jiggle out with perfect democracy. Every *independent quadratic way* a system can store energy — a velocity that appears as $\tfrac12 mv^2$, a spring coordinate that appears as $\tfrac12 kx^2$ — receives, on average, the **same** ration: $\tfrac12 k_BT$. This is why a single number, $k_BT$, is the natural currency of all of biophysics.

### Precisely

The **equipartition theorem**: in classical thermal equilibrium, each degree of freedom whose energy is a *quadratic* function of a coordinate or momentum contributes

$$\langle E\rangle = \tfrac12 k_BT$$

to the average energy. A point particle moving in three dimensions has three translational degrees of freedom ($\tfrac12 m v_x^2,\tfrac12 m v_y^2,\tfrac12 m v_z^2$), so its mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac32 k_BT$. A harmonic oscillator has *two* quadratic terms (one kinetic, one potential) and so averages $k_BT$ in total.

### Worked example

At body temperature $T=310$ K, the thermal quantum is

$$k_BT = (1.38\times10^{-23}\,\text{J/K})(310\,\text{K}) = 4.3\times10^{-21}\,\text{J},$$

or, per mole, $RT = N_A k_BT \approx 2.6$ kJ/mol $\approx 0.62$ kcal/mol. This is the size of one thermal kick — and it is why $k_BT \approx 0.6$ kcal/mol shows up everywhere as the yardstick against which binding energies, folding stabilities, and barrier heights are compared.

### Why it's true / how it works

For a coordinate $q$ whose energy is $E=\tfrac12 \alpha q^2$, the Boltzmann-weighted average $\langle \tfrac12\alpha q^2\rangle = \dfrac{\int \tfrac12\alpha q^2\, e^{-\alpha q^2/2k_BT}\,dq}{\int e^{-\alpha q^2/2k_BT}\,dq}$ is a standard Gaussian integral that evaluates to $\tfrac12 k_BT$ — **independently of the stiffness $\alpha$**. The mass or spring constant cancels, leaving only the temperature. That cancellation is the heart of equipartition: nature does not care *how* you store the energy, only *how many* independent quadratic slots there are.

### Where it connects

Equipartition fixes the thermal speed of molecules (used in **Einstein–Stokes** diffusion and the **Maxwell–Boltzmann** distribution), sets the magnitude of the random force in the **Langevin** equation, and provides the energy scale for every entropic-spring argument — the $k_BT$ in **entropic elasticity**, **worm-like-chain** stretching, and the **ideal chain**.

### Watch out

The theorem counts only *quadratic* degrees of freedom and only in the *classical* regime. A rigid rotor's tumbling counts; a stiff covalent stretch effectively does not at room temperature because it is quantum-frozen. Do not assume every atom contributes $3k_BT$ of vibrational energy — most bond vibrations are silent until the sample is hot.

### Numbers & nuance

The freeze-out condition is $\hbar\omega \gtrsim k_BT$. At 300 K, $k_BT$ corresponds to about $200\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ in spectroscopic units; vibrations stiffer than that (most C–H, C=O stretches sit at $1000$–$3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$) are frozen, while soft modes, rotations, and translations are fully thermally populated. This staircase of activating degrees of freedom as temperature rises is exactly what the temperature-dependence of heat capacity records — from the gas-phase $\tfrac32 R,\,\tfrac52 R,\,\tfrac72 R$ ladder to the Dulong–Petit $3R$ ceiling of a classical solid.

atoms.title: Chemical potential
atoms.summary: The free-energy cost of adding one more particle of a species — the master variable whose gradients drive diffusion, transport, binding, and phase separation.

depths.eli5: Chemical potential is the 'price' of one more molecule of something — how much free energy a system gains or loses when you add a single particle. Crowded, concentrated places have a high price; dilute places have a low price. Just as water flows downhill, particles flow from high chemical potential to low, and everything stops moving when the price is equal everywhere. That balance point is what we call equilibrium.
depths.core: The chemical potential μ_i of a species is the partial molar Gibbs free energy: the change in G when you add an infinitesimal amount of species i while holding temperature, pressure, and the other species fixed, μ_i = (∂G/∂n_i). For a dilute ideal solution it takes the simple logarithmic form μ_i = μ_i° + k_BT ln a_i, where a_i is the activity (≈ concentration for dilute, ideal cases) and μ_i° is a reference value. Two consequences make it the workhorse of biophysics: (1) species move down chemical-potential gradients, so a concentration ratio sets a driving free energy of k_BT ln(c_high/c_low); (2) at equilibrium the chemical potential of a species is equal across every phase and location it can reach — equal μ is what 'equilibrium' actually means.
depths.deep: The logarithmic concentration term is the same entropy of mixing that appears throughout statistical mechanics: spreading particles over more accessible volume raises entropy and lowers μ. Non-ideal interactions are folded into the activity coefficient γ (a_i = γ_i c_i/c°), which captures crowding, electrostatics, and excluded volume. Reaction equilibrium (ΔG° = −RT ln K), osmotic pressure, colligative properties, and phase coexistence are all just statements that the relevant chemical potentials are equal — μ is the single variable that unifies them.

resources.label: LibreTexts Chemistry — Physical & Theoretical Chemistry texts

atoms.art_prompt: two compartments at different concentrations connected by a channel, with a downhill free-energy slope labeled mu flowing from crowded to dilute

quiz.prompt: In thermodynamic terms, what is the chemical potential of a species, and what is true about it at equilibrium?
quiz.answer: It is the partial molar Gibbs free energy, μ_i = (∂G/∂n_i) — the free-energy cost of adding one more particle. At equilibrium μ_i is equal across every phase and location the species can reach.

quiz.prompt: From μ_i = μ_i° + RT ln a_i, derive the free energy released when one mole of an uncharged solute moves from a compartment at concentration c_high to one at c_low, and evaluate it for a tenfold concentration ratio at 310 K.
quiz.answer: ΔG = μ(low) − μ(high) = RT ln(c_low/c_high) = −RT ln(c_high/c_low); for c_high/c_low = 10, ΔG = −RT ln 10 = −(8.314)(310)(2.303) ≈ −5.9 kJ/mol ≈ −1.4 kcal/mol released. The reference μ° cancels because it is identical in both compartments, leaving only the concentration ratio.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Think of chemical potential as the **price of one more molecule**. Adding a particle to a crowded, concentrated region costs free energy (high price); adding it to a dilute region costs less (low price). Particles, like money, flow from where the price is high to where it is low — and all flow stops when the price is the same everywhere. That equal-price condition is precisely what equilibrium *is*.

### Precisely

The **chemical potential** of species $i$ is its partial molar Gibbs free energy,

$$\mu_i = \left(\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i}\right)_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}},$$

the free-energy change per particle added. For a dilute, ideal solution it reduces to the logarithmic form

$$\mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + k_BT\,\ln a_i,$$

where $a_i$ is the **activity** (the effective concentration; $a_i \approx c_i/c^\circ$ when dilute and ideal) and $\mu_i^\circ$ is a fixed reference value at the standard state.

### Worked example

A solute sits at 100 mM on one side of a membrane and 10 mM on the other. The free energy available to move one mole down this gradient is

$$\Delta G = RT\ln\frac{[\text{low}]}{[\text{high}]} = -RT\ln 10 \approx -5.9\ \text{kJ/mol} \approx -1.4\ \text{kcal/mol}.$$

The reference $\mu^\circ$ cancels — only the *ratio* of concentrations matters — and the negative sign says the move is spontaneous. This $\sim$1.4 kcal/mol per tenfold gradient is the energy that secondary transporters harvest.

### Why it's true / how it works

The $k_BT\ln a$ term is **entropy of mixing** in disguise. Letting particles explore more volume increases the number of accessible arrangements, raising entropy and therefore *lowering* the free energy per particle in dilute regions. Equating $\mu$ across regions is equivalent to maximizing total entropy subject to conservation of particles — the same variational principle behind the Boltzmann distribution.

### Where it connects

Chemical potential is the parent of an enormous amount of biophysics. Set it equal across a phase boundary and you get **osmotic pressure** and **phase coexistence** (the engine of biomolecular **condensates**). Add an electrical term and you get the **electrochemical potential**, whose equilibrium is the **Nernst** equation and the **GHK** voltage. Apply it to a reaction and you recover $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ and **binding** equilibria.

### Watch out

Use *activity*, not raw concentration, when interactions matter: $a_i = \gamma_i c_i/c^\circ$, with the activity coefficient $\gamma_i$ absorbing crowding, ion screening, and excluded volume. In the cytoplasm, where macromolecules occupy a large volume fraction, $\gamma$ can differ substantially from 1, and treating concentration as activity will misestimate driving forces.

### Numbers & nuance

At 310 K, $RT \approx 2.58$ kJ/mol and $RT\ln 10 \approx 5.9$ kJ/mol $\approx 1.4$ kcal/mol per *decade* of concentration. This is the same per-decade energy that reappears (divided by Faraday's constant) as the $\sim$61 mV/decade slope of the Nernst equation — a direct fingerprint that the membrane voltage is just a chemical potential wearing an electrical coat. Because the logarithm is gentle, even large concentration ratios translate into only a few $k_BT$: a $10^3$-fold gradient is worth merely $\sim$4.2 kcal/mol, which is why cells must chain several such gradients (or couple to ATP) to drive steeply uphill chemistry.

atoms.title: Electrochemical potential
atoms.summary: Chemical potential plus the electrical work z_iFψ — the true driving force for every ion across a membrane, and the quantity the Nernst equilibrium sets equal on both sides.

depths.eli5: An ion deciding which way to move across a membrane is weighing two things at once: how crowded it is (concentration) and how the voltage pushes or pulls its charge (electricity). The electrochemical potential simply adds those two pressures into one total 'urge to move.' The ion flows until that total is equal on both sides — even if the concentrations are still lopsided, because the voltage can exactly cancel the concentration push. That standoff is the resting state of a nerve cell.
depths.core: The electrochemical potential μ̃_i extends the chemical potential by adding the electrical work needed to bring a charged particle to a region at electrical potential ψ: μ̃_i = μ_i + z_iFψ = μ_i° + RT ln a_i + z_iFψ, where z_i is the ion's charge number and F is Faraday's constant. Ions flow down gradients of μ̃, not of concentration alone — a steep concentration gradient can be perfectly opposed by a voltage. Setting μ̃ equal on both sides of a membrane (the equilibrium condition) yields exactly the Nernst equation, E = (RT/z_iF) ln(a_out/a_in). When several ions and active pumps are involved, the steady (not equilibrium) balance gives the GHK voltage, and the stored μ̃ of protons is the proton-motive force that powers ATP synthesis.
depths.deep: Electrochemical potential is the bookkeeping that makes membrane bioenergetics quantitative. The proton-motive force is Δμ̃_H+/F = Δψ − (2.303RT/F)ΔpH, combining a voltage term and a pH (concentration) term into a single energy per charge — typically ~150–200 mV across a mitochondrial or bacterial membrane, enough to drive the rotary ATP synthase. Secondary active transporters (symporters/antiporters) work by letting one ion run down its μ̃ gradient to drag another up its own, conserving total μ̃ change ≤ 0. Every 'active' transport step is ultimately a statement about the sign of a sum of electrochemical potentials.

atoms.art_prompt: an ion at a membrane with two stacked arrows — a concentration arrow and a voltage arrow — summing into one net driving-force arrow that goes to zero at balance

quiz.prompt: A potassium ion is more concentrated inside a cell than outside, yet at the resting potential there is no net K+ flux. How does the electrochemical potential explain this?
quiz.answer: The outward concentration force on K+ is exactly cancelled by the inward electrical force from the negative-inside membrane voltage. Net flux is zero when the electrochemical potential μ̃_K is equal inside and out — i.e. when the voltage equals the K+ Nernst potential — even though the concentrations remain unequal.

quiz.prompt: Set the electrochemical potential of an ion equal across a membrane and derive the Nernst equation. Then write the proton-motive force and evaluate its magnitude for Δψ = 150 mV and ΔpH = 1 at 310 K.
quiz.answer: Equilibrium means μ̃_in = μ̃_out: μ° + RT ln a_in + zF ψ_in = μ° + RT ln a_out + zF ψ_out. Cancel μ° and rearrange: zF(ψ_in − ψ_out) = RT ln(a_out/a_in), so the equilibrium voltage E = ψ_in − ψ_out = (RT/zF) ln(a_out/a_in) — the Nernst equation. For protons the stored energy per charge is the proton-motive force pmf = Δμ̃_H+/F = Δψ − (2.303RT/F)ΔpH. At 310 K, 2.303RT/F ≈ 61 mV. With Δψ = 150 mV and a ΔpH worth another 61 mV (the two terms add for the way mitochondria orient their gradient), pmf ≈ 150 + 61 ≈ 211 mV ≈ 0.21 V, i.e. F·0.21 ≈ 20 kJ/mol of free energy per proton transported.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

A charged particle facing a membrane is pushed by **two** forces at once: the crowding force of concentration, and the electrical force of voltage acting on its charge. The **electrochemical potential** adds these two into a single number — the ion's total urge to move. The ion flows until that total is equal on both sides, which can happen *even while the concentrations stay lopsided*, because the voltage can exactly cancel the concentration push. That precarious balance is the resting state of every nerve and muscle cell.

### Precisely

The **electrochemical potential** of ion $i$ adds electrical work to the chemical potential:

$$\tilde\mu_i = \mu_i + z_iF\psi = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln a_i + z_iF\psi,$$

where $z_i$ is the charge number (e.g. $+1$ for K$^+$, $-1$ for Cl$^-$), $F = 96{,}485$ C/mol is Faraday's constant, and $\psi$ is the local electrical potential. Ions move down gradients of $\tilde\mu$, not of concentration alone.

### Worked example

Potassium is $\sim$140 mM inside a neuron and $\sim$5 mM outside, a 28-fold gradient pushing K$^+$ *out*. Yet at rest there is essentially no net K$^+$ current. The reason: the inside-negative membrane voltage pulls K$^+$ *in* with exactly enough electrical force to cancel the chemical push. Equality of $\tilde\mu_{\text{K}}$ inside and out is reached when the voltage equals the K$^+$ Nernst potential, $\approx (RT/F)\ln(5/140) \approx -89$ mV.

### Why it's true / how it works

Setting $\tilde\mu_i$ equal on the two sides *is* the Nernst equation. Writing $\tilde\mu_{\text{in}} = \tilde\mu_{\text{out}}$, the reference $\mu^\circ$ cancels and rearranging gives

$$E = \psi_{\text{in}}-\psi_{\text{out}} = \frac{RT}{z_iF}\ln\frac{a_{\text{out}}}{a_{\text{in}}}.$$

So the membrane voltage is nothing more than a chemical potential wearing an electrical coat: the $\sim$61 mV-per-decade Nernst slope is exactly the $RT\ln 10$ per-decade chemical-potential energy divided by $F$.

### Where it connects

Electrochemical potential is the hinge between molecular thermodynamics and bioenergetics. Its equilibrium gives the **Nernst** potential; its multi-ion steady state gives the **GHK** voltage and feeds **Hodgkin–Huxley** excitability; its stored proton form is the **proton-motive force** that the **chemiosmosis** chapter converts into ATP. **Secondary active transporters** run one ion downhill in $\tilde\mu$ to drag another uphill.

### Watch out

Distinguish *equilibrium* from *steady state*. A single ion at equilibrium has equal $\tilde\mu$ and zero flux (Nernst). A resting membrane with several leak channels and active pumps is in a *steady state* with ongoing fluxes that cancel — described by GHK, not by a single Nernst potential. Conflating the two is the most common error in electrophysiology.

### Numbers & nuance

The proton-motive force combines voltage and pH into one energy per charge,

$$\text{pmf} = \Delta\psi - \frac{2.303\,RT}{F}\Delta\text{pH},$$

with $2.303RT/F \approx 61$ mV at 310 K. A typical mitochondrion runs $\Delta\psi \approx 150$–180 mV with a $\Delta$pH worth another $\sim$30–60 mV, totaling $\sim$200 mV $\approx 19$ kJ/mol per proton — and roughly three to four protons flowing back down this gradient turn the rotary ATP synthase enough to make one ATP. The entire economy of the cell is denominated in electrochemical potential.

atoms.title: Law of mass action
atoms.summary: At equilibrium the ratio of products to reactants is fixed by a single number K, and that number is set exponentially by the standard free-energy change — the bridge between thermodynamics and concentrations.

depths.eli5: Mix some chemicals and they react until they reach a standstill — not because everything is used up, but because the forward and backward reactions run at the same speed. At that balance point the amounts of products and reactants settle into a fixed ratio called the equilibrium constant K. A reaction that 'wants' to go forward (releases free energy) has a big K; one that barely budges has a small K. The connection is exponential: a little more free energy released multiplies K a lot.
depths.core: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the law of mass action says the reaction quotient Q = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b moves until it reaches a fixed value, the equilibrium constant K. Thermodynamics fixes that value: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0 with Q = K, giving ΔG° = −RT ln K. The standard free-energy change is the logarithm of the equilibrium constant scaled by RT. Kinetically, K is also the ratio of the forward and reverse rate constants, K = k_f/k_r, so the same equilibrium can be reached from either direction.
depths.deep: The exponential sensitivity, K = exp(−ΔG°/RT), is the same Boltzmann factor that weights microstates: products and reactants are two macrostates whose populations sit in ratio exp(−ΔG°/RT). Because RT ≈ 2.6 kJ/mol at body temperature, each extra 5.9 kJ/mol (one RT·ln10) shifts K by a full factor of ten. This is why catalysts — which lower the barrier, not ΔG° — change the speed but never the final ratio, and why coupling an unfavorable reaction to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG° ≈ −30 kJ/mol) can multiply its equilibrium constant by ~10^5.

atoms.art_prompt: a balance beam with reactant flasks on one pan and product flasks on the other, settling at a tilt set by a free-energy gauge labeled delta-G-naught, with an exponential curve mapping delta-G to K

quiz.prompt: What does the equilibrium constant K describe, and how is it related to the standard free-energy change of a reaction?
quiz.answer: K is the fixed ratio of products to reactants (each raised to its stoichiometric power) reached at equilibrium. It is related to the standard free-energy change by ΔG° = −RT ln K, equivalently K = exp(−ΔG°/RT).

quiz.prompt: Starting from ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, derive the relation ΔG° = −RT ln K, then compute ΔG° for a reaction with K = 1000 at 310 K.
quiz.answer: At equilibrium the reaction has no driving force, ΔG = 0, and the quotient Q equals its equilibrium value K. Substituting: 0 = ΔG° + RT ln K, so ΔG° = −RT ln K. For K = 1000 at 310 K: ΔG° = −(8.314)(310) ln(1000) = −(2577)(6.908) ≈ −17.8 kJ/mol. The reaction is favorable by about 18 kJ/mol, three RT·ln10 steps for three decades of K.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Let a reversible reaction run and it reaches a **standstill** — but not because the reactants are exhausted. The forward and reverse reactions simply end up running at the *same rate*, so the net change stops. At that point the amounts settle into a fixed ratio, the **equilibrium constant** $K$. A reaction that strongly favors products has a large $K$; one that barely proceeds has a small $K$.

### Precisely

For a general reaction $a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}$, define the **reaction quotient**

$$Q = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}.$$

The system evolves until $Q$ reaches the fixed value $K$. Thermodynamics pins that value through

$$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q,$$

and at equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$ with $Q = K$, which gives the central result

$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K.$$

### Worked example

A reaction has $K = 1000$ at body temperature. Its standard free-energy change is

$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln 1000 = -(8.314)(310)(6.908) \approx -17.8\ \text{kJ/mol}.$$

Three decades of $K$ cost three $RT\ln 10 \approx 5.9$ kJ/mol steps — about 18 kJ/mol of favorable free energy.

### Why it's true / how it works

The relation is a **Boltzmann factor in disguise**. Products and reactants are two macrostates, and their equilibrium populations sit in the ratio $K = \exp(-\Delta G^\circ/RT)$ — the same exponential weighting that governs energy levels in statistical mechanics. Equivalently, $K = k_f/k_r$: equilibrium is where the forward rate constant times reactant concentrations equals the reverse rate constant times product concentrations.

### Where it connects

Mass action is the parent of nearly every concentration law in biophysics. Apply it to binding and you get the **dissociation constant** $K_d$; to enzyme saturation, the **Michaelis** constant; to acids, $\mathrm{p}K_a$ and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation; to membranes, the **Nernst** equilibrium. The logarithmic form is the same $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ that connects every one of them to the underlying free energy.

### Watch out

A **catalyst lowers the barrier, not $\Delta G^\circ$** — it speeds the approach to equilibrium but cannot change $K$ or the final ratio. Also, $Q$ and $K$ must be written with activities (or properly referenced concentrations); using raw molarities for charged or crowded species can shift the apparent $K$.

### Numbers & nuance

Because $RT \approx 2.6$ kJ/mol, every additional $RT\ln 10 \approx 5.9$ kJ/mol multiplies $K$ by ten. This exponential lever is how cells perform 'impossible' chemistry: coupling an unfavorable step to ATP hydrolysis ($\Delta G^\circ \approx -30$ kJ/mol) multiplies its equilibrium constant by roughly $10^5$, turning a reaction that would never proceed into one that runs to near-completion.

atoms.title: Arrhenius equation
atoms.summary: Reaction rates rise exponentially with temperature because only the small Boltzmann-weighted fraction of molecules carrying enough energy to clear the activation barrier can react.

depths.eli5: Chemical reactions usually have to climb an energy 'hill' before they can happen. Only molecules that happen to be moving fast enough — carrying enough energy — make it over. Heat the system and a much larger fraction of molecules have that energy, so the reaction speeds up fast. The Arrhenius equation captures this: the rate depends exponentially on how high the hill is and how hot it is. A roughly 10°C rise often doubles a biological rate.
depths.core: The Arrhenius equation, k = A e^(−E_a/RT), expresses how a rate constant k depends on temperature. E_a is the activation energy (the barrier height), R is the gas constant, T the absolute temperature, and A is the pre-exponential factor (collision frequency × orientation). The exponential term is exactly the Boltzmann fraction of molecules with energy at least E_a. Taking logs gives ln k = ln A − E_a/(RT), a straight line of slope −E_a/R when ln k is plotted against 1/T — the standard way to measure an activation energy experimentally.
depths.deep: Arrhenius is the empirical, phenomenological face of transition-state theory: the Eyring equation k = (k_BT/h) exp(−ΔG‡/RT) gives the same exponential temperature dependence but resolves the barrier into enthalpic (ΔH‡) and entropic (ΔS‡) parts, with A absorbing k_BT/h and exp(ΔS‡/R). The pre-factor A is weakly temperature-dependent, so over a narrow biological range the simple Arrhenius form is an excellent fit. Enzymes act by lowering E_a (stabilizing the transition state), which — because the dependence is exponential — buys enormous rate enhancements: dropping E_a by ~6 kJ/mol multiplies the rate roughly tenfold at body temperature.

atoms.art_prompt: an energy-landscape hill with reactant valley on the left and product valley on the right, a labeled activation-energy barrier E_a, and two Boltzmann population curves (cold vs hot) showing far more molecules above the barrier when hot

quiz.prompt: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(−E_a/RT), what does each symbol mean, and why does raising temperature increase the rate?
quiz.answer: k is the rate constant, A the pre-exponential factor (collision frequency and orientation), E_a the activation energy (barrier height), R the gas constant, and T absolute temperature. Raising T increases the Boltzmann fraction e^(−E_a/RT) of molecules carrying at least the barrier energy, so more collisions are reactive and the rate climbs exponentially.

quiz.prompt: A reaction has an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol. By what factor does its rate change when temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K (its Q10)? Show the ratio.
quiz.answer: The pre-factor cancels in a ratio: k(310)/k(300) = exp[−E_a/R · (1/310 − 1/300)] = exp[(E_a/R)(1/300 − 1/310)]. With E_a/R = 50000/8.314 = 6014 K and (1/300 − 1/310) = 1.075×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹, the exponent is 6014 × 1.075×10⁻⁴ = 0.647, so the ratio = e^0.647 ≈ 1.9. The rate nearly doubles — the classic Q10 ≈ 2 of biochemistry.

atoms.lesson:
### Intuition

Most reactions must climb an **energy hill** before products can form. Only molecules that happen to carry enough energy make it over the top. Because the fraction of energetic molecules grows steeply with temperature, modest heating speeds reactions dramatically — a roughly $10^\circ$C rise often doubles a biological rate.

### Precisely

The **Arrhenius equation** gives the temperature dependence of a rate constant:

$$k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT},$$

where $E_a$ is the **activation energy** (barrier height), $A$ the **pre-exponential factor** (collision frequency times the chance of correct orientation), $R$ the gas constant, and $T$ the absolute temperature. The exponential is exactly the **Boltzmann fraction** of molecules with energy $\ge E_a$.

### Worked example

For $E_a = 50$ kJ/mol, going from 300 K to 310 K multiplies the rate by

$$\frac{k(310)}{k(300)} = \exp\!\left[\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{300}-\frac{1}{310}\right)\right] = e^{0.647} \approx 1.9.$$

The rate nearly doubles — the familiar $Q_{10}\approx 2$.

### Why it's true / how it works

Taking the logarithm linearizes it: $\ln k = \ln A - E_a/(RT)$. Plotting $\ln k$ against $1/T$ yields a straight line of slope $-E_a/R$, which is how activation energies are measured. The exponential form is inherited directly from the Boltzmann distribution: the probability a molecule has at least the barrier energy falls off as $e^{-E_a/k_BT}$ per molecule, $e^{-E_a/RT}$ per mole.

### Where it connects

Arrhenius is the **empirical cousin of the Eyring equation** from transition-state theory, $k = (k_BT/h)\,e^{-\Delta G^\ddagger/RT}$, which splits the barrier into enthalpy and entropy. Both share the same exponential temperature law. **Enzymes** work by lowering $E_a$ (stabilizing the transition state), and **Kramers theory** refines the pre-factor $A$ to include friction and barrier curvature.

### Watch out

The pre-factor $A$ is itself weakly temperature-dependent, so a perfectly straight Arrhenius plot is an approximation valid over a limited range. Biological systems also break the rule above ~40°C, where proteins denature and rates *fall* despite rising temperature — the barrier picture no longer describes an intact catalyst.

### Numbers & nuance

Because the dependence is exponential, small changes in $E_a$ have outsized effects: at body temperature, lowering $E_a$ by one $RT\ln 10 \approx 5.9$ kJ/mol multiplies the rate tenfold. This is the lever enzymes pull — a barrier reduction of 30–50 kJ/mol corresponds to rate enhancements of $10^5$ to $10^9$, turning geological-timescale reactions into millisecond ones.

atoms.title: Osmotic pressure
atoms.summary: A solute lowers the solvent's chemical potential, so pure solvent pushes across a semipermeable membrane until a pressure builds that exactly restores the balance — a pressure proportional to solute concentration.

depths.eli5: Put pure water on one side of a barrier that lets water through but not sugar, and sugar-water on the other. Water flows toward the sugary side, as if trying to dilute it. It keeps going until the extra height (pressure) of liquid on the sugary side pushes back hard enough to stop the flow. That pushback is the osmotic pressure, and it grows in proportion to how many dissolved particles there are — not what they are. This is why cells swell in fresh water and shrivel in brine.
depths.core: Osmotic pressure Π is the pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop pure solvent from flowing into it across a semipermeable membrane. For a dilute solution it follows the van 't Hoff relation Π = cRT, where c is the total molar concentration of dissolved particles (osmolarity), R the gas constant, and T temperature — strikingly similar in form to the ideal-gas law. The driving force is the chemical potential of the solvent: dissolving solute lowers the solvent's chemical potential by RT ln(x_solvent), and solvent flows from high to low potential until an opposing pressure raises it back to equality.
depths.deep: Osmotic pressure is a direct consequence of equating the solvent chemical potential across the membrane: μ_solvent(pure) = μ_solvent(solution) + V_m ΔP at equilibrium, where the pressure work V_mΔP compensates the entropic lowering RT ln x_solvent ≈ −RT·x_solute. With x_solute ≈ c·V_m one recovers Π = cRT. It is a colligative property: it counts particles, so it dissociates electrolytes (van 't Hoff factor i) and is the same physics behind boiling-point elevation and freezing-point depression. In cells, the large osmotic pressure from impermeant macromolecules and ions must be balanced — by rigid walls in plants and bacteria, by active ion pumping and the Donnan equilibrium in animal cells — or the cell lyses.
